name: Agriculture and commodity trading
systems: Grain and ag-retail accounting ERPs for elevators and cooperatives: AGRIS (Greenstone/Cultura, PC 1984, Windows 2000-03), Agvance (SSI, 1981 origin, Windows mid-1990s), AgTrax/TraxView (1996), Merchant Ag (Ever.Ag/EFC), AgVision, Primetics, AMIC, CORETech (Cultura/Constellation portfolio)

Commodity trading and risk management (CTRM) for traders and processors: ION Openlink Endur, ION TriplePoint (Triple Point Technology, 1993), ION Agtech, ION Allegro, Softmar (chartering), iRely i21 (successor to older iRely origination/grain products)
Large-enterprise ERP estates at global merchants (e.g. ADM worldwide ERP programme), often with SAP Commodity Management
Workarounds around the core: spreadsheets for analytics and non-physical trades, email/paper for post-trade execution, paper books at palm-fruit dealers
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The core is 1980s-90s Windows client-server rather than mainframe, and its vendors keep modernising it in place (SQL, hosted versions) while overlays like Bushel and Covantis work around it. That makes the category less locked-in on platform and skills than mainframe-heavy categories. The paper, email and spreadsheet workarounds are more severe than typical.

s1.why: Primary vendor histories show the leading systems in both tiers predate 2005 as on-prem PC/Windows client-server. AGRIS was a grain elevator accounting system in 1981, went to PC in 1984 and to Windows in 2000-03, with SQL added only in 2014-16. Agvance (SSI, founded 1981, Windows suite mid-1990s) reports 3,800+ ag retail locations and about 50% of the CropLife Top 100, which shows it dominates. On the CTRM side, TriplePoint (1993) and Openlink Endur (1990s) are also pre-2005. Caveats: none of this is mainframe or IBM i, and Agvance has offered a cloud (SKY) version since 2016, so part of that base is now hosted.

s2.why: The only primary evidence is one firm. ADM's 10-Ks show a worldwide ERP and legacy-system replacement still 'in phases over the next several years' from FY2016 through FY2024, with no deployments in 2024. That is a general ERP programme at a single top merchant. The Adaptive CTRM case study ('extended period of time') is an anonymous vendor case. I found no evidence of 7+ year contracts or of typical replacement timelines for the dominant grain accounting systems (AGRIS, Agvance, AgTrax) or for CTRMs across the category.

s3.why: There is quantified evidence that the dominant players work around their systems with email, paper and re-keying. Consensys, citing FAO/IPPC ePhyto, says more than 275M emails a year are exchanged to process about 11,000 ocean grain shipments, and the six largest merchants formed Covantis to cut rekeyed entries. An Eka/Quoreka survey found 66% of commodity firms rely primarily on spreadsheets for analysis versus 12% on CTRM, and an agri CTRM case study retires an Excel-based solution for non-physical trades. Caveats: the Eka survey is a vendor survey of only 50 executives across ag, chemicals and energy, and the Covantis reduction figures are projections. The email-volume figure is the strongest single datapoint.

s4.why: The only support is a specialist recruiter (Cititec), who describes a 'small pool' of people who know E/CTRM systems, and a Capco consultancy paper on Endur implementation skills. Both lean toward energy trading, and both are secondary or self-interested. I found nothing on skills scarcity for AGRIS, Agvance or other grain accounting systems, and no COBOL/RPG angle, since no midrange grain system was confirmed.

reasons_to_stay: Grain accounting systems embed scale-ticket, contract, settlement, warehouse-receipt and patronage logic tied to local regulation (e.g. USWA licensing, farmer tax exemptions), so replacement means rebuilding compliance-critical workflows

Global merchants' ERP/CTRM replacements run for years in phases (ADM: FY2016 to FY2024 and still not finished), with material control risk (ADM's FY2024 10-K reports a material weakness in internal control and no ERP deployments that year)
Vendors keep modernising in place (AGRIS added MS SQL in 2014-16, Agvance added the SKY cloud version in 2016), which lowers the pressure to switch
Consolidated vendor ownership (Constellation/Volaris via Cultura; ION across Openlink, TriplePoint, Allegro and Agtech) keeps products supported long-term
Integration overlays (e.g. Bushel integrates with existing grain accounting systems instead of replacing them) extend the life of the legacy core
Scarce specialist implementation skills (Endur and E/CTRM) raise project risk and cost

name: Airline reservations and passenger service
systems: IBM ACP / TPF / z/TPF mainframe transaction platform (origin of PARS/IPARS reservation applications)
Sabre host reservation system (American Airlines/IBM, built 1960, live 1964) and its airline-hosted successor SabreSonic Customer Sales & Service
Amadeus Altéa Suite (Reservation, Inventory, Departure Control), hosted PSS for full-service carriers
Navitaire Open Skies (1994, HP3000) and New Skies (conversions from 2005), LCC PSS now owned by Amadeus
Travelport (Worldspan/Galileo/Apollo) z/TPF hosting of airline internal reservation systems (Delta, United, Northwest historically)
SITA Gabriel (Unisys-based) and SITA Horizon PSS
Videcom VRS (UK, regional/small carriers)
Radixx (LCC PSS, Sabre-owned since 2019)
Airline in-house legacy PSS (e.g. ANA domestic system operating since 1988)
Cryptic / green-screen agent terminals and Sabre Scribe scripts layered on the host
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Less legacy-locked at the runtime than a typical enterprise category, because the two dominant PSS vendors (Amadeus by 2018, Sabre mostly by 2024) have already moved their own hosts off the mainframe and run them as multi-tenant hosted services. More locked at the contract and data-model level than most: a vendor switch is a multi-year, airline-wide cutover through IATA PNR, EDIFACT and interline plumbing.

s1.why: The dominant hosts all came from mainframes. Sabre was built on IBM mainframes from 1960 and went live in 1964. Amadeus Altéa ran on the Amadeus TPF complex: Qantas went live on Altéa Reservation in 2002, and Amadeus did not retire its TPF mainframes until 2017-2018. Navitaire Open Skies launched in 1994 on HP3000. Primary sources from both main vendors confirm this: Sabre's FY2025 10-K says its platform 'evolved from mainframe-based transaction processing', and Amadeus has published its own account of retiring TPF. Caveat for the study: those same sources show the dominant installed base is no longer on mainframe. Amadeus has run fully on open systems since 2018 and is moving to Azure. Sabre moved about 90% of its workloads to Google Cloud by Feb 2024. What is legacy today is the application lineage (PNR and EDIFACT data models, cryptic command interfaces), not the runtime.

s2.why: Several primary sources across vendors show multi-year replacements and long contracts. Southwest's own release says its move to Altéa took about 3 years (2014-2017) and 1,500+ people. Qantas moved to Altéa module by module from 2002 to 2008, and signed a 10-year deal in 2007. LATAM signed a 10-year Sabre PSS contract in 2015 and implemented through 2018. ANA plans to replace a domestic PSS that has run since 1988, with migration over FY2025-26. Sabre's 10-K puts hosted airline contracts at roughly 3-10 years with minimum volumes. Even the vendors' own re-platforming took years: Amadeus's mainframe exit took about 2,000 effort-years, and Sabre missed its own 2023 mainframe-exit target.

s3.why: The only concrete evidence is one RPA vendor press release (Automation Anywhere's call-center bot that re-keys refunds and vouchers), which is vendor marketing. There is also anecdotal material on Sabre Scribe and cryptic-command scripting. The DataArt screen-scraping source returned 403 and could not be read, and no evidence of spreadsheet workarounds was found. Cryptic terminal use is a native interface, not proof of a workaround. Nothing quantifies how widespread this is across Altéa, Navitaire or SabreSonic users.

s4.why: IBM's Redpaper does say 'specialized TPF skills can be scarce'. But that is a platform vendor talking about z/TPF, and the two largest PSS vendors have mostly left z/TPF: Amadeus fully by 2018, Sabre about 90% by 2024. Navitaire is .NET and cloud-hosted. For the dominant installed systems, airline staff need Altéa, Navitaire or Sabre configuration skills and cryptic-command fluency, and no source shows those are scarce. The CIO Dive mainframe skills-gap piece is secondary and not specific to this category. Scarcity is real only for the remaining TPF holdouts (some Travelport-heritage hosts, in-house carrier systems).

reasons_to_stay: Cutover risk is existential. A PSS swap touches every booking, ticket and check-in. Southwest needed 3 years and 1,500+ people, and Qantas phased modules over 2002-2008.
Long hosted contracts with minimum annual volume commitments (Sabre: 3-10 years) and exit costs.
Interline, codeshare, alliance and GDS connectivity, and IATA EDIFACT/ticketing/BSP integrations, are built around the incumbent host.
Performance: z/TPF is purpose-built for high-volume seat-inventory transactions, and IBM positions it as unique for airline workloads.
Incumbents are modernizing in place (Sabre moving off mainframe to cloud; Amadeus Nevio offer/order with Finnair, Lufthansa Group, AF-KLM, BA, Saudia). That lowers the urgency to switch vendor.
Agents and airport staff are trained on cryptic commands and scripts, so retraining costs are high.
Revenue management, loyalty, DCS and accounting systems are tightly coupled to PSS data feeds.

name: Capital markets trading, clearing and brokerage back-office
systems: Broadridge Brokerage Processing Services (BPS), the US broker-dealer back office. Its lineage goes back to the ADP brokerage services group (1962), and Broadridge still runs it on mainframe infrastructure that Kyndryl operates
63 moons (formerly Financial Technologies) ODIN broker front-office/trading terminal (India, 1998)
63 moons exchange trading, clearing and settlement stack (DOME framework 2002; MCX platform since 2003)
ASX CHESS clearing, settlement and subregister system (Australia, live since 1994)
NSE NOW broker trading front end (India, discontinued 2020)
MPC (Micro Piranti Computer) S21 / S21+ BOFIS broker back office (Indonesia)
FSS FLEX core securities system (Vietnam)
TCS BaNCS for market infrastructure and brokerage. It is the replacement platform at MCX rather than a legacy incumbent
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software. Its cores are regulator-gated network utilities (exchanges, clearing houses, depositories), and every link to them must be re-certified, so failed replacements like ASX CHESS cost hundreds of millions and are public. But the end-user broker layer already has well-funded cloud-native challengers (Apex, Alpaca, DriveWealth, Clear Street), which makes it less locked than core banking.

s1.why: Primary sources show pre-2005 on-prem or mainframe cores for the dominant systems in two major markets. Broadridge's FY2026 10-K says Kyndryl runs its mainframe and midrange operations, with that deal extended to 2031 and a new mainframe lease starting 2027. Broadridge's brokerage processing goes back to 1962 and it serves the 15 largest US wealth providers. The RBA describes ASX CHESS, live since 1994, as a 29-year-old system. ODIN (1998) and DOME (2002) date from the same era. One gap: the SEA cores (MPC S21, FSS FLEX) have no verified ship date.

s2.why: Two national clearing systems have quantified, primary-source replacement timelines. ASX started replacing CHESS in 2016, wrote off A$245-255m in 2022, and the program now runs to about 2029. MCX's move from 63 moons to TCS took from Feb 2021 to Oct 2023, with quarterly extension fees rising from Rs 15 cr to Rs 125 cr, and SEBI fined MCX for the late disclosure. Broadridge's mainframe outsourcing runs to 2031, and it carries $819m of deferred client conversion and start-up costs. One caveat: the strongest cases are market-infrastructure utilities. For broker back offices, multi-year conversions are inferred from Broadridge's deferred costs, not measured.

s3.why: The only evidence is secondary. The TRADE quotes Acuiti's head of research saying most sell-side firms still use spreadsheets, email and chat, but the survey numbers are paywalled and unverified. The evidence is industry-wide and is not tied to Broadridge, CHESS, ODIN or any named core. No source shows re-keying or screen-scraping against a specific dominant system.

s4.why: The one primary source covers a single system. The RBA (confirmed) says ASX has significant key-person risk on CHESS because of the skills the ageing system needs, including its programming language, and that vendors had not announced support plans past 2025. Nothing comparable was found for Broadridge BPS, ODIN or the SEA back offices. General COBOL-scarcity figures come from modernization vendors, not from this category.

reasons_to_stay: Regulators gate cutover. SEBI asked MCX on 28 Sep 2023 to hold its planned 3 Oct go-live, and the RBA/ASIC oversee CHESS milestones, so switching takes regulatory sign-off and mock trading.
Replacement failure is costly and public. ASX wrote off A$245-255m in 2022 after Accenture found the new software 63% complete. Boards that saw this choose the incumbent extension.

The incumbent gains pricing power during migration. MCX's 63 moons support fees rose from Rs 15 cr to Rs 125 cr a quarter while the TCS platform slipped, and staying still looked safer than a rushed cutover.
Conversion costs are sunk and multi-year. Broadridge carries $819m of deferred client conversion costs amortised over service terms, and clients would face the same cost again to leave.

Network integration: a broker back office links to the exchange, the depository (KSEI C-BEST in Indonesia, VSDC in Vietnam, CDSL/NSDL in India), bank RDN accounts and the clearing house. Every link has to be re-certified.
The current system works. ASX's 2022 release said current CHESS remains secure and stable and is performing well.

name: Card issuing and payments processing
systems: Fiserv (ex-First Data/PaySys) VisionPLUS and FirstVision: IBM mainframe, COBOL/CICS/VSAM credit card management system
Fiserv Optis: North American credit card processing platform (ex-First Data)
TSYS TS2 / TS1 (Global Payments Issuer Solutions, being sold to FIS): mainframe cardholder processing system
ACI Worldwide BASE24: HP/Tandem NonStop switch and authorization system for ATM/POS/card
FIS BASE2000 (Kordoba): mainframe card processing
HPS PowerCARD: card issuing/acquiring suite (on-prem licensed)
OpenWay Way4: licensed card issuing/acquiring platform, dominant in Vietnam
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. A handful of 1990s-era mainframe and NonStop platforms (TS2, VisionPLUS/Optis, BASE24) process most cards at the largest issuers, under 3-to-10-year processing contracts with penalties and scheme certifications. But cloud processors (Marqeta, Thredd, Pismo, Zeta) have already won the greenfield fintech segment, so the lock-in is concentrated at incumbent banks.

s1.why: The issuer platforms that dominate the installed base all predate 2005 and run on mainframe or NonStop hardware. TSYS TS2 (1994) and VisionPLUS (late 1995, descended from CardPac in 1982) both run on COBOL/JCL/CICS mainframes, and VisionPLUS carries 600M+ cards. FIS BASE2000 is also a mainframe product. ACI's own history page says BASE24 was developed in the mid-1970s for Tandem NonStop, and it had 131 customers by 1986. Fiserv's 10-K confirms that Optis, FirstVision and VisionPLUS are its card platforms. These products span the big three processors (TSYS, Fiserv/First Data, FIS) and the leading switch, not one vendor. Two caveats: the technology detail comes from Mphasis, a secondary consulting blog, and the research's 1982 BASE24 date is wrong (ACI says mid-1970s).

s2.why: Primary filings show multi-year replacements at the largest issuers. Bank of America's 2012 TSYS deal had a six-year minimum term plus a conversion of about 24 months, so roughly 8 years end to end. JPMorgan Chase took a perpetual TS2 license (TSYS 8-K). TSYS 10-Ks say issuer processing contracts generally run three to ten years, with early-termination penalties and annual revenue minimums. Global Payments' 10-K describes the same structure. Two caveats: the 3-to-10-year range does not by itself prove that 7+ years is typical, and the 'usual 30 months' migration time comes from OpenWay's CEO, a vendor. The multi-year conversion prong is clearly met for tier-1 issuers.

s3.why: The only evidence is a marketing blog from Rivero, a dispute-software vendor. It says issuers reconcile Mastercard dispute fund movements with manual spreadsheets and tribal knowledge. That covers one adjacent function (disputes and chargebacks), not the core processing system, and it is a vendor selling the fix. No regulator, independent survey or practitioner study was found showing re-keying or screen-scraping around TS2, VisionPLUS or Optis.

s4.why: The BMC 2025 Mainframe Survey has 45% of financial-services respondents citing staffing and skills as a priority. That covers all financial-services mainframes, not card processing, and the blog gives no sample size. VisionPLUS and BASE24 job posts asking for 8-10 years of experience show the skill is niche, but they are anecdotal and do not prove scarcity. The Mphasis source says nothing about skills. India-based training shops and offshore vendors (Mphasis, Synechron) appear to keep a VisionPLUS bench, so the pool is narrow rather than shown to be shrinking.

reasons_to_stay: Long contracts with annual minimums and early-termination penalties (Global Payments 10-K). The Bank of America TS2 deal had a 6-year minimum term.
Conversions are risky multi-year projects: 24 months for Bank of America, and a 'usual 30 months' for a core card migration per OpenWay.
Mainframe platforms are proven at very large scale (600M+ cards on VisionPLUS versions) with high availability for authorization.
Scheme certifications, regulatory reporting and fraud and collections integrations are built up over decades around the core.
Incumbents are modernizing in place. Fiserv is re-engineering Optis (Celent), which lowers the urgency to switch.
Licensed in-house options (TS2 perpetual license) let large banks keep control without a platform change.

name: Construction project accounting
systems: Sage 300 Construction and Real Estate (formerly Timberline Office), Windows client-server on Pervasive/Actian Zen database
Trimble Viewpoint Vista (US/global construction ERP, SaaS and client-server)
Trimble Viewpoint Spectrum (formerly Dexter + Chaney)
Trimble Viewpoint Jobpac Connect (ANZ, formerly Jobpac)
Foundation Software (FOUNDATION construction accounting)
CMiC (Computer Methods International Corp) single-database construction ERP
Computer Guidance Corp eCMS (runs exclusively on IBM i / OS/400)
Jonas Construction Software and other Constellation/Jonas construction brands
Access Coins / COINS (UK and Ireland, Progress OpenEdge ABL based)
Generic tier-one ERPs used by large contractors (Oracle E-Business Suite 11i/R12, SAP), plus UK tier-two Eque2, RedSky, Causeway
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software because decades of job-cost, certified/union payroll and WIP/surety reporting history sit in pre-2005 client-server cores (Timberline, Viewpoint, COINS). It is less locked than mainframe categories because those cores run on mainstream Windows/SQL, get hosted, and are routinely bolted onto by cloud overlays instead of ripped out.

s1.why: Primary sources cover the dominant US/UK installed base. Sage's own KB confirms Sage 300 CRE (Timberline, from 1971) still runs as Windows client-server on the Pervasive/Actian file engine, and Sage advises against VPN because a dropped connection can lock files or damage data. Trimble's 2018 8-K describes Viewpoint (about 8,000 customers, 46% of the ENR 400) as selling client-server solutions. Foundation (1985), CMiC (1974), Dexter + Chaney/Spectrum (1981), Jobpac (late 1980s), COINS on Progress OpenEdge and CGC eCMS on IBM i all predate 2005. The caveat is that no dominant pre-2005 construction product was found in SEA or India. There the base is SAP, Oracle or generic local packages.

s2.why: Construction News confirms multi-year, failure-prone replacements at UK tier-one contractors. Kier's Oracle ERP went from a GBP 30m budget (2014) to about GBP 90m and went live about two years late (Sep 2018), with a GBP 7.3m writedown. Balfour Beatty wrote down GBP 21m, and Interserve wrote off GBP 17m and abandoned its rollout. These are generic Oracle and Microsoft ERP projects at a handful of the largest firms, not migrations off the dominant construction-specific products. No source shows 7+ year contracts. Mid-market Sage 300 CRE and Vista migrations appear to take months, not years. Sage supports only 2 to 3 versions at a time, which forces upgrades but not replacement.

s3.why: The best evidence is the independent JBKnowledge ConTech survey (2019 and 2020). Where construction apps do not integrate, firms move data manually (49-53%) or by spreadsheet (44-48%), and only 5% say all their apps integrate. Accountants are named among the groups that still rely on spreadsheets. The survey covers the industry's whole app stack and does not tie re-keying to Sage 300 CRE, Vista or Spectrum. Evidence tied to specific systems is vendor marketing only: Field Materials says it removes re-keying of POs and invoices into Vista, and Siteline says pay-app billing runs on spreadsheets.

s4.why: Scarcity is shown only for niche products: a COINS developer post asks for Progress OpenEdge ABL plus day-one COINS expertise, and CGC eCMS is tied to IBM i. The dominant US products (Sage 300 CRE, Vista and Spectrum on Windows/SQL) have a large reseller and consultant channel (Aktion, RKL, Kerr and many regional Sage partners) and hundreds of open job postings. No quantified shortage was found. The scarce skill is product-specific admin and report-writing knowledge, which no source measures.

reasons_to_stay: Job costing, payroll and union/certified payroll are embedded in decades of data. Construction payroll (prevailing wage, union fringes, multi-state) is hard to replicate.
Failed enterprise ERP replacements are well publicised: Kier's Oracle project grew from GBP 30m to about GBP 90m, and Interserve abandoned its rollout with a GBP 17m writedown.
The Trimble Viewpoint, Sage and Access Coins ecosystems sell bolt-on modules and hosted versions, so customers can move to cloud hosting without re-platforming.
Point solutions (Field Materials, Siteline, Briq) sit on top of Vista and Sage 300 CRE, which lowers pressure to replace the core.
Some vendors (e.g. CMiC) still support on-premise deployment, and construction tolerates on-prem more than most industries.
WIP schedules, surety and bonding reports, and auditors' CFMA-style reporting are built around existing report formats.
Thin margins (Vietnam contractors under 10% gross) and cyclical cash flow limit IT budgets.

differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. s1.why: The installed base is dominated by Fiserv (31% of credit unions, 42% of banks) and Jack Henry (12% of credit unions, 21% of banks), per the Kansas City Fed. Their flagship cores run on IBM Power midrange hardware and are pre-2005 designs. Jack Henry's own 10-Ks describe SilverLake as IBM i based and Episys as IBM AIX based. Episys descends from Symitar (founded 1984, acquired 2000). Fiserv Premier on IBM i came with the 1995 ITI acquisition and had about 2,000 customers in 2009 (IT Jungle). Caveats: the ship dates come from secondary sources, and this is US-heavy. India's PACS ERP (2022) and Germany's consolidated agree21 are newer, and Philippine rural banks are moving to SaaS.

s2.why: Jack Henry's FY2021 10-K, a primary source, says outsourced core contracts typically run 7+ years with minimum guaranteed payments. The Kansas City Fed survey finds 61% of banks have stayed with their core provider for more than 10 years. Atruvia took 3 years and 60 series migrations to move 341 German cooperative banks onto agree21. India's PACS ERP rollout is a 5-year programme (2022-23 to 2026-27). Counter-evidence: Fiserv's FY2013 10-K cites 3-5 year account-processing terms. A single US credit union conversion usually takes 9-24 months (industry blogs).

s3.why: Most of the evidence is anecdotal or comes from vendors. TechCrunch's 2015 piece on Oradian says MFIs run on Excel or pen and paper. PearlPay's CEO made the claims about Philippine rural banks. A Vietnamese trade article says People's Credit Funds lack customer information systems. Industry blogs mention re-keying online applications into the core. The one quantified figure (MIX/CGAP: 41% of MFIs on manual MIS) is unverified. No primary survey measures spreadsheet or re-keying dependence on the dominant US credit union or community bank cores.

s4.why: The skills evidence covers the platforms, not this category. In Fortra's 2026 IBM i Marketplace Survey, IBM i skills shortage was the top concern, and a Procern analysis puts more than 72% of IBM i developers over 50. That bears on IBM i cores such as SilverLake, Premier and CIF 20/20. But these cores are maintained by their vendors and mostly delivered as outsourced service bureaus, so member institutions rarely employ RPG or COBOL staff themselves. No source shows a scarcity of Episys PowerOn or PowerBuilder/FoxPro BPR skills specifically. The ILO-OJK finding is about a user-skills gap, not scarce programmers.

name: Core banking
systems: FIS Systematics (IBM mainframe, COBOL; Systematics Inc. founded 1968, now FIS)
Jack Henry SilverLake (IBM System/38 then AS/400 / IBM i, RPG; developed 1986-87)
Jack Henry CIF 20/20 (IBM System/36 then AS/400, RPG/400; lineage to Jack Henry's original 1977 system)
Jack Henry Core Director (Windows client/server)
Jack Henry Symitar Episys (credit unions)
Fiserv Premier, Precision, Signature, Cleartouch, Portico, DNA (Fiserv account processing)
Temenos Transact / T24 (GLOBUS lineage 1988, T24 launched 2003)
Finastra Fusion Equation (Kapiti, IBM AS/400) and Fusion Midas (1975-76, IBM System/32, RPG II)
Silverlake Axis SIBS (IBM AS/400 / Power Systems; Silverlake founded 1989)
Oracle FLEXCUBE (i-flex, 1997)
Infosys Finacle (1999)
TCS BaNCS (FNS origin, acquired by TCS 2005)
SAP for Banking (replacement core at CBA 2008-2012)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Core banking is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software: it is the regulated system of record. 61% of US banks have kept the same core provider for 10+ years, and failed migrations draw public fines (TSB, GBP48.65M). The lock-in is softer in Asia, where most installed cores are 1997-2003 Java/Oracle products (Finacle, FLEXCUBE, T24) rather than mainframe or RPG.

s1.why: Primary, quantified evidence covers the dominant installed base. Kansas City Fed: Fiserv, Jack Henry and FIS together serve more than 70% of US banks (2022). Jack Henry's FY2025 10-K counts 520 SilverLake and 260 CIF 20/20 banks, both on IBM midrange (System/38, System/36, AS/400 lineage, 1977 to 1987), plus 170+ Core Director client/server banks. Outside the US the leading cores also predate 2005: Temenos T24 (GLOBUS 1988, T24 2003, 950+ core clients), FLEXCUBE (1997), Finacle (1999), Equation/Midas (AS/400, 1976) and Silverlake SIBS (AS/400). Caveat: Fiserv and FIS give no core first-ship years or client counts, and Temenos, Finacle and FLEXCUBE are 1990s/2000s on-prem stacks rather than mainframe.

s2.why: Stickiness is well quantified, but the sign's two tests are only partly met. On contracts, primary data fails the 7+ year bar: ICBA's 2020 survey puts most community bank terms at 4 to 8 years, a negotiator cites a 5.6-year average, and Jack Henry's typical outsourcing term is six years. On replacement duration, the evidence is anecdotal tier-1 cases: CBA took five years and over A$1B (CEO via iTnews), TSB's Proteo4UK cutover failed, and Jack Henry plans a ~15-year rewrite with 10-15 years of IBM i coexistence. A typical US community bank conversion takes about a year. Quantified tenure is strong: 61% of banks have kept the same core provider for more than 10 years (KC Fed), more than a third for 20+ years, and about three quarters stay to avoid conversion (ICBA). That tenure is lock-in, not proof of multi-year replacement.

s3.why: The only primary source is one bank anecdote: the SDNY Citibank/Revlon opinion describes a manual three-field 'wash account' workaround in Flexcube that misdirected about $894M. Survey figures on spreadsheets and manual processes (e.g. Wolters Kluwer's 88% of US lenders using spreadsheets) come from vendors, cover regulatory and risk work, and do not tie the workaround to the core system. No regulator or quantified source shows re-keying or screen-scraping around the dominant cores.

s4.why: Evidence is secondary: a BMC vendor blog citing Reuters (43% of banking systems on COBOL), mainframe-vendor survey claims, and GAO-25-107795, which covers federal agencies, not banks. RPG/IBM i and COBOL skills for SilverLake, CIF 20/20 and Systematics are plausibly scarce. But the large non-US installed base (Temenos T24, Finacle, FLEXCUBE, BaNCS) runs on Java/jBASE/Oracle stacks with deep Indian and SEA talent pools, so scarcity is not shown across the category.

reasons_to_stay: The risk of a failed migration is existential and publicly punished: TSB's 2018 migration led to GBP48.65M in FCA and PRA fines and multi-day outages for 5.2M customers.
Replacement takes years and costs a lot: CBA's program ran five years and cost over A$1B against an original A$580M four-year forecast.
Vendors themselves expect 10-15 years of coexistence. Jack Henry says most customers will keep running IBM i cores for ten or fifteen years and it will keep supporting them.
Outsourced core contracts auto-renew at multi-year terms (Jack Henry's typically run six years; Fiserv cites high renewal rates), and termination fees and deconversion costs build switching friction.

The core is the system of record for deposits, loans and the GL, with decades of business rules held only in code. The Citi Flexcube case shows how much process knowledge sits in manuals and operator habits.
Regulator expectations on operational resilience and outsourcing (PRA/FCA, MAS TRM, OJK, RBI) add approval and testing overhead to any switch.
Integration lock-in: payments, digital banking, cards and regulatory reporting are all wired to the existing core's interfaces.

Victoria (AU) Courtlink, a mainframe case management system installed about 30 years before 2018
Washington State Judicial Information System (JIS, formerly DISCIS), built in-house since 1988

Germany: JUDICA, EUREKA, EUREKA-Fach, forumSTAR, web.sta, MESTA and GO§A, all being replaced by GeFa
Tyler Technologies Odyssey (now Enterprise Justice), general release 2003
Journal Technologies eCourt / eSeries
Justice Systems FullCourt / FullCourt Enterprise
equivant (Constellation Software) CourtView and JustWare/JWorks
Court Contexte (COTS base of Hawaii JIMS)
NSW JusticeLink (KAZ Group/Telstra)
Singapore CrimsonLogic EFS (2000), replaced by eLitigation (2013)
India eCourts Case Information System (CIS) by NIC
Malaysia e-Kehakiman CMS/eFS
Philippines eCourt

Thailand Court of Justice CIOS
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More locked-in than typical enterprise software, because each jurisdiction is a single sovereign buyer. It works on annual appropriations, has statutory record and judicial-consensus constraints, and depends on many interfaces to police, prosecutors and DMV. Rollouts take a decade. It is less mainframe-bound than banking or tax, since much of the US moved onto 2003-era vendor platforms (Tyler, Journal Technologies) and most Asian judiciaries built post-2007 systems.

s1.why: Primary sources show pre-2005 on-prem cores for the dominant systems in the largest markets. US federal CM/ECF (every federal court, run as localized per-court applications) is 'nearly three decades' old per the US Courts' own 2026 release. Tyler Odyssey, the leading US state-court platform, had general release in Q3 2003 as on-prem client-server (Tyler FY2003 10-K). Germany's Länder systems (JUDICA, EUREKA, forumSTAR, MESTA) predate the 2017 GeFa replacement project (BMJV). UK Libra was procured in 1996-2002 (NAO). Caveats: the Hawaii mainframe detail dates from about 2012 and may be retired, and most Asian systems are post-2005 builds (India CIS 2007, Malaysia e-Kehakiman 2011, PH eCourt 2013, SG eLitigation 2013). So this is strong for the US, UK, EU and AU only, not SEA or India.

s2.why: Several primary sources across separate jurisdictions show decade-scale replacements. Maryland's statewide MDEC rollout ran from fall 2014 to May 2024, which the Maryland Judiciary itself describes as county by county over 10 years. Germany's GeFa started in 2017 and targets 2030 (BMJV). CM/ECF replacement has been studied since the 18F reports and is still in pilot in 2026, with completion two to three years out. HMCTS reform ran from 2016 to 2025 (NAO). Victoria chose Journal Technologies in 2019 and criminal go-live came in 2026. This is a pattern across buyers, not one anecdote. California CCMS ($260m to $1.9bn, then terminated) is seen only in a search snippet.

s3.why: The evidence is real but anecdotal and old. The Hawaii RFP (about 2012, one state) says data passed between DC Crim and HAJIS must be manually re-entered, alongside paper, fax and spreadsheets. Computerworld (2018, secondary) reports Victoria's manual processes on top of nine CMSs. OSR found UK Common Platform staff typing free text instead of result codes, which is a data-quality problem in a new system, not a legacy workaround. No quantified or cross-jurisdiction source shows re-keying or spreadsheet dependence across the dominant installed base (Odyssey, eCourt, CM/ECF).

s4.why: No opened court-specific source shows that skills are scarce. The support is indirect. Hawaii's (about 2012) Adabas/Natural/COBOL-CICS stack, the Georgetown JIF roadmap's general remark that COBOL makes court modernization cost-prohibitive, and general COBOL-shortage surveys (Computerworld) are not judiciary data. The court-specific items (a Courthouse News quote about a retired programmer, the Berrien County COBOL/Natural review) could not be opened, and my search did not surface them either. The dominant current platforms (Tyler Odyssey on .NET, Journal Technologies eCourt on Java/web, CM/ECF on Perl/web) do not need a scarce mainframe skill set. Scarcity applies to the residual in-house mainframe tier only.

reasons_to_stay: Replacements fail or run long and over budget. California CCMS ($260m to $1.9bn, then terminated), UK Libra (£146m bid rose to £318m, core application missed its 2001 deadline), HMCTS Common Platform rollout paused over performance problems
Statewide migrations take a decade or more (Maryland MDEC 2014-2024, Germany GeFa 2017-2030), so courts keep the old system running in parallel for years
Courts depend on many interfaces with police, prosecutors, criminal history repositories, NCIC and DMV (Hawaii lists AG, HCJDC, NCIC, DOT and police interfaces), so every interface must be rebuilt
Statutory record-keeping and data integrity. Common Platform free-text results corrupted official criminal statistics (OSR), which raises perceived risk
Funding is fragmented: Michigan's 242 trial courts have 165 local funding sources. Budgets are annual appropriations, not capital programmes
Judicial independence and consensus. A single judge can stop a modernization project (Georgetown JIF roadmap)
Few vendors and lock-in to incumbents (Tyler, Journal Technologies, equivant) with long statewide contracts

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital EHRs are more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software on age and replacement time: M/MUMPS and 1990s client-server cores, 10-year contracts, and multi-billion-dollar multi-year cutovers. But the dominant vendor (Epic) is gaining share and keeps its skill pipeline fed, so skill scarcity is weaker than in mainframe categories.

s1.why: The three vendors that hold about 80% of US acute hospitals (KLAS 2026: Epic 43.7%, Oracle Health/Cerner 21.9%, MEDITECH 14.7%) all run cores from before 2005. Epic Chronicles is an M/MUMPS database (Epic founded 1979) usually run on-prem or Epic-hosted, and it is not cloud-native. Cerner Millennium is a late-1990s client-server design. MEDITECH dates MAGIC to 1979-82 and Client/Server to 1994, and its 10-K and anniversary page confirm these. Outside the US the pattern repeats: VistA (40+ years), SAP IS-H (1990s), Sunrise at SingHealth (1998), HBCIS (about 1990) and Malaysia THIS (1999). One caveat: Cerner's Millennium ship date was not confirmed from a primary source. Oracle's 2025 cloud EHR is still ambulatory-only.

s2.why: GAO (primary, which I opened) confirms the VA replacement. The IDA estimate is $49.8B: 13 years of implementation plus 15 years of sustainment. Deployments paused from April 2023 to December 2024, and not all centers will be done by the May 2028 contract end. This is a sector-wide pattern, not one case. NHS trusts sign 10-year Epic EPR contracts: Lewisham and Greenwich £52M to 2036, with go-live a year after signing; Somerset and Dorset £222M, 2026-2036. Cabinet Office caps EPR terms at 10 years, so 10 is the norm. Others: Queensland's HBCIS replacement at about 7 years, SingHealth's Sunrise extended to 2029, and SAP IS-H support stretched to 2030/2033.

s3.why: The main source is a peer-reviewed scoping review (Blijleven et al., JMIR 2022), which includes 62 of 737 studies. It documents workarounds such as paper persistence, duplicate documentation and side systems. But it covers EHRs in general and does not tie prevalence to the dominant vendors. Most of the workarounds it describes are clinical-workflow coping. It does not quantify spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping caused by an aging core. The rest of the evidence is anecdotal or regional: Selayang going manual after a crash, Vietnam running paper and electronic records in parallel, and manual matching in Indonesia. The PMC page was CAPTCHA-blocked, so I confirmed the review's scope only through PubMed search results.

s4.why: The only primary, quantified source is VA testimony (March 2023): about 70% of VA MUMPS programmers are retirement-eligible. That covers one system (VistA), which is already being retired. For the dominant vendors, Epic and Oracle Health, scarcity is real but comes from vendor-gated certification and demand from new installs, not a dying skill base. Epic trains new graduates in-house. The figures here come from recruiters, such as the claim of 15 open Epic roles per certified analyst, which is secondary marketing. I found no primary evidence of skill scarcity for MEDITECH, Cerner CCL or SAP IS-H.

reasons_to_stay: High switching cost. MEDITECH's 10-K example: a typical 150-bed hospital pays a $3M product fee plus a $1M implementation fee, then about $30K a month.
Patient-safety and go-live risk. VA paused rollout for 20 months, and 75% of surveyed users said the new system did not make them as efficient as possible (GAO-25-106874).
Program cost overruns. VA's EHR estimate went from about $10B to $37-50B life-cycle.
Data migration from decades of clinical records. VistA holds 15M+ lines of MUMPS code, and VA says modernizing would mean rewriting it almost from scratch.
Epic's network effects (Care Everywhere, MyChart) and the KLAS-ranked suite lock in large systems. Epic's share keeps rising.
Regulatory and certification requirements (ONC, NHS DSPT, Kemenkes PMK 24/2022 RME and SATUSEHAT integration) favour incumbent certified vendors.
Public-sector budget and procurement constraints. Malaysia MOH cites budget limits, Queensland's procurement was delayed by a conflict-of-interest probe, and Vietnam's small bidders under-deliver.
Retraining large clinical workforces and the downtime risk of a cutover.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Less locked-in than a typical enterprise category. Most installed systems are mid-market products on Windows/SQL Server or Progress, so they can be replaced in 12 to 18 months, and Epicor and Infor are pushing customers to their own cloud versions. Pockets of real lock-in remain: UniVerse/Pick (Eclipse) and RPG (A+), plus decades of contract-pricing logic.

s1.why: The systems that dominate the installed base all have pre-2005 on-prem or midrange cores, across both of the big vendors. Epicor Eclipse shipped in 1990 on the UniVerse multivalue (Pick) database with a character UI. Infor A+ is RPG on IBM i, from Daly & Wolcott (1988). Infor SX.e is a Progress 4GL product from NxTrend, before 2005. Prophet 21 was an established Windows/Unix vendor (company founded 1967) when Activant bought it in 2005. Regional tails are older still: Pronto Xi 1984, Dynamics GP 1990s. This rests on several independent sources, not one vendor. Each source is a company history (Wikipedia, IT Jungle), not a census of installs. Still, the dominant installed products are not in doubt.

s2.why: No source shows contracts of 7 years or more. The main multi-year example is one firm, Wesco, with a $500M program. The checker found that this program is described as ecommerce, supply-chain and backend modernization, not an ERP replacement. The Crestwood partner blog gives 12 to 18 months for mid-market distribution migrations, which is under the multi-year bar for the typical buyer. The Epicor P21 on-prem phase-out (final release May 2028, active support ends 30 Jun 2029) and Dynamics GP end of support (2029) show that vendors hold long tails, but that is vendor policy, not measured replacement duration.

s3.why: The evidence is quantified but indirect. Conexiom's 74%-of-orders-with-issues figure is a vendor claim. It describes inbound orders arriving by email or PDF and being re-keyed. That is a buyer-side channel problem, not something tied to a particular ERP. The Distribution Strategy Group survey (n=233, Q1 2026) shows 55% of distributors run ERP, CRM, ecommerce and analytics that are not integrated. It does not measure spreadsheet use or re-keying against named legacy ERPs. Figures like '20-40% of rep time on manual order handling' come from vendor blogs. Re-keying is plausible and widespread, but no primary source links it to the dominant systems (P21, Eclipse, SX.e).

s4.why: The Fortra 2026 IBM i survey (n=315, 69% name skills a top concern) is solid. It only covers RPG/IBM i products (Infor A+, JD Edwards World), which are a minority of this installed base. The dominant systems run on other platforms. P21 is Windows/SQL Server, and its admins are hired from a normal Microsoft talent pool. Eclipse runs on UniVerse/Pick, and SX.e on Progress OpenEdge. No skills-scarcity data was found for UniVerse/Pick or Progress 4GL. Scarcity is plausible for Eclipse and SX.e but not shown.

reasons_to_stay: Deep vertical logic: contract and customer-specific pricing, rebates, multi-branch inventory, counter sales and buying-group integrations accumulated over decades (P21, Eclipse built for electrical/HVAC/PVF).
Heavy customizations and integrations to ecommerce, EDI and WMS make replacement risky. Advisors cite 12 to 18 months for mid-market migrations.
Vendors keep the old systems running. Epicor says the P21 on-prem phase-out is not end-of-life, and active support runs to June 2029.
Thin distribution margins and fear of order and fulfilment disruption during cutover.
Users are productive on character-based and green-screen order entry.
Vendor-sanctioned cloud paths (Epicor Cloud, Infor CloudSuite, Business Central) let firms re-host without re-platforming.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Manufacturing ERP is more legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category because the core is wired into plant-floor equipment, MES, OEM EDI and traceability records, so cutover means risking a production stop. That keeps decades-old SAP ECC, IBM i RPG and Progress 4GL systems running long after vendor deadlines, even though SMB manufacturers are moving quickly to cloud MRP.

s1.why: The dominant installed systems all have pre-2005 on-prem or midrange cores. SAP ECC 6.0 (2006) runs on the R/3 base that launched in 1992, and most ECC users have not moved off it: DSAG's 2025-26 survey has only 37% of German-speaking ECC users planning to reach S/4HANA by 2027. The mid-market lineages are older still. MAPICS/Infor XA dates from 1977 on IBM midrange, BPCS/Infor LX from the early 1980s on IBM i, JD Edwards World runs RPG on System/38 and AS/400, Baan/Infor LN dates from the 1980s-90s, QAD MFG/PRO from the mid-1980s in Progress 4GL, and Epicor Vantage/Vista from the 1990s client-server era. Ship dates come from encyclopedic or vendor-history sources, but they hold across every major vendor and are not disputed. Cloud-native systems (Plex, NetSuite) are the minority.

s2.why: The quantified evidence covers one vendor. In DSAG's survey (198 leaders, Dec 2025 to Jan 2026), 37% plan to switch from ECC to S/4HANA by end-2027, about half by 2030, and 4% by 2033. SAP has extended ECC support to 2027, then 2030 at a premium, then a 2033 private-edition option. So the SAP programmes do run for years. Across ERP in general, Panorama's 2024 ERP Report gives a 15.5-month median project and says more than half finished on schedule. That cuts against 'multi-year' for typical mid-market manufacturing replacements. No source shows 7+ year contracts. JDE E1 premier support to 2033 is a support horizon, not a contract term.

s3.why: Spreadsheet workarounds are plausible and widely reported, but the cited evidence is a vendor survey (Qlector) of a small sample of Slovenian manufacturers, in which 50% supplement ERP planning with Excel or paper. Other figures are vendor or analyst claims that blame missing MES coverage rather than legacy ERP: IoT Analytics says 54% of plants used pen and paper or spreadsheets in 2024, and Galorath says 96% use Excel for cost estimation. No large-sample primary source ties re-keying or screen-scraping to the dominant legacy ERP systems.

s4.why: There is a quantified primary survey, but it covers the platform rather than the category's dominant system. In Fortra's 2026 IBM i Marketplace Survey (n=315), 69% name IBM i skills a top concern, up from 60% in 2025 and ahead of security for the first time in nine years. The secondary LiminalArc report adds that 72% of IBM i developers are over 50. This applies to the IBM i/RPG installed base (Infor XA/LX, JDE World, BPCS), which is a mid-market slice. It also spans every industry, not only manufacturing. For SAP ECC, the dominant system, the only evidence is DSAG citing 'skills shortages', and those are S/4 migration skills, not scarce ECC/ABAP skills. ABAP talent is still relatively plentiful.

reasons_to_stay: Business process change is the top barrier to leaving ECC (49% of ASUG respondents). Customizations come second (44%) and organizational inertia third (37%).
Vendors keep extending support: SAP ECC mainstream runs to 2027, extended to 2030 at +2 points, and a private-edition transition option to 2033. JD Edwards EnterpriseOne premier support runs to 2033.
Migration capacity is short. DSAG cites skills shortages, parallel transformation projects and budget limits as reasons to delay.
Deep shop-floor integration (MES, PLCs, EDI with OEM customers, quality and traceability records) makes cutover risky for plants that cannot stop production.
Sunk cost and stability: decades-old RPG/Progress systems work, and replacement implementations still have a median of 15.5 months (Panorama 2024).

systems: SAP R/3 / SAP ERP 6.0 (ECC) FI-CO general ledger
Oracle E-Business Suite General Ledger (Oracle Financials, 11i / R12 / 12.2)
Oracle PeopleSoft Financials 9.2 General Ledger
Oracle JD Edwards World (IBM i / AS/400) and JD Edwards EnterpriseOne General Accounting
Oracle Hyperion Financial Management (HFM) / Hyperion Enterprise for consolidation and close
Microsoft Dynamics GP (Great Plains Dynamics)

Spreadsheet-based close (Excel) layered on top of the ERP
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The installed base sits on 1990s cores (SAP ECC, Oracle EBS, JD Edwards) kept in place by audit, SOX and statutory-reporting risk, but close-overlay tools and fast mid-market migrations let firms work around the GL rather than being locked in, so it is less locked than the core banking or mainframe categories.

s1.why: The installed GL systems that dominate the category all shipped before 2005 as on-prem client-server or midrange software: SAP R/3 (1992, ECC 6.0 in 2006 on the same lineage), Oracle EBS Financials (late 1980s), PeopleSoft, JD Edwards World on AS/400, Great Plains Dynamics (1993) and Hyperion Enterprise/HFM. Gartner gives a number for how much of the base still runs that core. It estimates over 60% of SAP customers remain on ECC6 on-premises (The Register, Feb 2025). The dates come mostly from Wikipedia, but they are not in dispute. One caveat: newer mid-market buyers increasingly start on cloud GLs (NetSuite, Intacct), so this holds for the installed base, not for new sales.

s2.why: The base is slow to move, and this is quantified only for SAP. Gartner expects about 40% of today's ECC customers to still run ECC in key areas in 2030, 15 years after S/4HANA shipped. But per-project replacement is not clearly multi-year. ASUG's 2024 survey (n=208) puts the average S/4HANA migration at 1.5 years, ranging from 4 months to 6 years. Mid-market GL moves (GP to Business Central, or to newer AI GLs) are measured in months. Oracle's support dates to 2037 show vendors extending support, not how long replacement takes. No evidence of 7+ year contracts was found.

s3.why: Spreadsheet-heavy close work is widely reported, but the quantified sources are vendor material: Ledge's benchmark (n=100, 94% use Excel in the close) and BlackLine's own 10-K, where BlackLine has a commercial interest. The Gartner controllership survey (n=497, via CFO Dive) measures error rates, not spreadsheet use. None of these sources ties the workarounds to the legacy GL cores. Excel-based close is just as common on modern cloud ERPs, so this sign does not separate legacy systems from modern ones.

s4.why: Scarcity evidence exists only for the IBM i / RPG segment (JD Edwards World and homegrown AS/400 GLs). Fortra's 2025 IBM i survey, a vendor survey, has 60% citing skills as a concern. ASNA's retirement projection is a migration vendor's assumption. No evidence was found of scarce SAP FI-CO/ABAP or Oracle EBS skills, and SAP and Oracle are the dominant cores. ASUG notes only that migration consultants will be in demand, which is about S/4HANA skills, not legacy ones.

reasons_to_stay: The GL is the audited system of record. Changing it touches SOX/ICFR controls, audit trails and statutory reporting, and migrations run 4 months to 6 years (ASUG 2024).
Vendors keep extending support. Oracle Premier Support for EBS 12.2, JDE E1 9.2 and HFM 11.2 runs to at least Dec 2037. SAP ECC extended maintenance runs to 2030, with options to 2033.
Heavy customization. 44% of ASUG members cite customizations and 49% cite business-process change as barriers (The Register, Nov 2025).
Gartner says many SAP customers cannot build a compelling business case for S/4HANA.
Local statutory, tax and e-invoicing localizations (e.g. India GST in Tally, SE Asian tax packs) are already built and certified in the legacy product.
Close-overlay tools such as BlackLine, FloQast and Numeric let firms fix close pain without replacing the GL, which delays a core swap.
Third-party support (Rimini Street, Spinnaker) and Sustaining Support let firms run frozen versions indefinitely.

name: Government benefits and social security
systems: In-house COBOL mainframe benefit systems (US SSA: over 60 million lines of COBOL as of 2010)
State unemployment insurance (UI) mainframe systems from the 1970s and 1980s, mostly COBOL (US)
Centrelink ISIS (Income Security Integrated System) on Rocket/CCA Model 204 (Australia)
DWP ICL/Fujitsu VME mainframe benefit suite (JSAPS, Pension Strategy Computer System launched 1988), COBOL from the 1980s (UK)
Deutsche Rentenversicherung rvSystem/rvDialog, COBOL on z/OS mainframes (Germany)
IBM/Merative Cúram Social Program Management (client-server/Java SPM suite, 1990s origin)
Deloitte-built state integrated eligibility systems for Medicaid and SNAP (US)
CPF Board COBOL mainframe applications (Singapore, partly modernised to Java under BEACON from 2018)
EPFO Field Office Application Software, decentralised regional databases (India, replaced by CITES 2.01 in 2026)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. National benefit cores are bespoke government COBOL/mainframe builds that hard-code statutory payment rules, and they cannot pause payments to migrate. That makes rewrites decade-long and politically risky. There is no off-the-shelf SaaS replacement market.

s1.why: Several primary audit sources date the dominant national cores to before 2005. SSA OIG counted over 60M lines of COBOL as of June 2010. GAO-23-105478 found state UI systems 7 to about 50 years old, many of them 1970s-80s COBOL mainframes. NAO dates DWP's Pension Strategy Computer System to 1988 on ICL/Fujitsu VME. Centrelink ISIS runs on Model 204, first deployed 1972. That covers the largest payers in US, UK and AU, so the evidence is not tied to one vendor. One caveat: there is no evidence for the ASEAN and India cores (BPJS, VSS, SSO, SSS/GSIS, KWSP), and Cúram/Deloitte eligibility systems are newer client-server or Java builds.

s2.why: Primary, quantified evidence of multi-year replacement. NAO (Feb 2024) says Universal Credit migration will finish at least 6 years later than planned, with some of it running to 2028. Australia's WPIT was a 7-year program of about A$1.5B, and by June 2020 only 13% of ISIS had been decommissioned. The Model 204 licence ran on an 11-year deal (2003-2014). DWP's VME re-platforming took 2016-2021. GAO found 6 of 8 sampled states still mid-modernisation of UI as of Feb 2023.

s3.why: The strongest primary evidence covers a single system. NAO (Sept 2021) found DWP State Pension administration has 'limited automation'. Caseworkers review at least three systems and set prompts by hand, and this led to 134,000 underpayments and a manual review of about 273,000 cases. In the US, GAO only implies paper-based UI processes, citing a reduction in paper as a modernisation gain. The ANAO finding that ISIS business rules are undocumented is about missing documentation, not workarounds. No quantified source shows spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping across the dominant systems in several countries.

s4.why: Several primary audit bodies document the skills gap directly. GAO-25-107795 (government-wide, covering SSA among others) says COBOL/assembly have a dwindling pool of skilled people and agencies pay a premium for staff or contractors. GAO-23-105478 says most sampled states lacked staff with the necessary expertise for UI systems. SSA OIG (2012) recommended planning for the loss of COBOL programmers. ANAO (via iTnews) flagged Model 204 skills running down at Services Australia. This is mostly US evidence, with AU from a secondary report of the audit.

reasons_to_stay: Payment rules are hard-coded and undocumented. Services Australia has no documentation of the age-pension business rules inside ISIS, so moving them is risky (ANAO via iTnews).
Replacements have failed or slipped. Australia scrapped a A$191M entitlements engine in 2023 because it ran slower than Model 204. Universal Credit is at least 6 years late.
Errors in benefit payments are politically costly. Deloitte system rollouts brought backlogs (Kentucky: 50,000 cases, 600+ defects) and wrong notices (KFF Health News).

The old cores are stable and pay out at huge scale: DWP about USD 202B a year, ISIS about 62M transactions a day. Rehosting COBOL (DWP VME-R, DRV Baden-Württemberg, CPF BEACON) is often preferred to a rewrite.
Benefit rules change every year by statute, so agencies have to keep paying while they migrate, which forces long parallel running.
Procurement and funding cycles (federal matching funds, multi-year budgets) favour large incumbent integrators.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is less locked than core banking or mainframe tax because the leading platforms run on mainstream Java or .NET stacks with vendor SaaS migration paths, few hard skills shortages, and 3-to-5-year contracts. It is more locked than typical SaaS categories because statutory workflows, fee schedules and decades of parcel and case history sit in proprietary schemas held by about 90,000 fragmented local buyers (in ASEAN, by a few national platforms).

s1.why: Several dominant installed cores are shown by primary sources to date from before 2005 and to run as on-prem client-server or midrange systems. The Connected Places Catapult study of UK planning software found Idox, which over 90% of UK councils use, set up as a local client on planners' machines with document management on a local server (it calls these 'legacy planning software'). San Diego's audit says its homegrown PTS was designed in the late 1990s and went live in 2001. NYC DOB calls BIS a mainframe. Branson runs Naviline on an AS/400 with DB2 and has done for 20 years. Tidemark dates to 1984 and Hansen to the 1980s. Caveat: the two leading US products, Tyler EnerGov (about 2002) and Accela Automation (early 2000s, web-based Java), are borderline on the 2005 cut-off and are not mainframe.

s2.why: Independent government audits across different vendors show multi-year replacements. California's BreEZe was proposed in 2009 at $28M, cost $96M by 2015 and covered only about half its 37 entities (State Auditor 2014-116). San Diego's move from PTS to Accela was due to go live in May 2017, slipped to February 2020, and its budget grew from $10.9M to $17.7M (City Auditor 19-011). NYC DOB NOW has been replacing the BIS mainframe in stages since about 2016 and the two still run side by side. Singapore runs CORENET X in parallel with CORENET 2.0 from 2H 2023. Caveat: the contract terms seen are 3 to 5 years, not 7 or more (Oxford's 3-year minimum, San Diego's 5-year Accela contract, Idox 3-year extensions). Small councils often switch in 12 to 18 months. The evidence comes from large jurisdictions.

s3.why: The Catapult sector study rests on interviews across the UK planning industry and covers the dominant installed base (Idox, Northgate/NEC). It reports that planners are 'forced' into manual workarounds such as copying and pasting between programmes. Planning officers manage cases in Excel sheets and manual lists instead of the system's tracking tool, and GIS data is re-keyed by hand. In the US the evidence is anecdotal. Richmond's auditor found elevator tracking done manually after the EnerGov rollout, and Branson builds its Naviline reports in Excel. It is strong for the UK and weaker for the US and ASEAN. It is qualitative and has no percentage figures.

s4.why: The only quantified source is generic to IBM i. Fortra's 2026 survey found 69% of IBM i shops name skills a top concern, but that applies only to the AS/400 slice of the base (Naviline/H.T.E.). San Diego's audit gives a primary anecdote of key-person risk: the City over-relied on the one PTS architect from the 1990s, and losing that institutional knowledge delayed the Accela migration. Most dominant platforms (Accela, Tyler EnerGov, Idox Uniform, NEC, Infor Pathway) run on mainstream Java, .NET or Oracle/SQL Server stacks. No source shows a scarcity of skills specific to permitting.

reasons_to_stay: Decades of permit, parcel and case history plus scanned documents sit in proprietary schemas. The Catapult report describes a UK council that judged retrieving its own data from a vendor too risky because of contract complexity, so it chose to upgrade and extend instead.
Tight integration with finance, utility billing, GIS and cashiering in integrated suites (Naviline, Pathway, Tyler). Replacing permitting alone breaks fee and parcel links.
Large replacement programmes have failed publicly: California's BreEZe went from $28M to $96M and covered about half its planned scope. This makes councils and boards risk-averse.
Statutory clocks, fee schedules and local code rules are configured into workflows over years, and must be rebuilt and re-validated.

Procurement and budget cycles: UK councils often roll Idox Uniform maintenance forward in 3-year extensions (e.g., Tameside 2024-27, Dartford 2025-28, per Contracts Finder search results) instead of re-platforming.
National mandates in ASEAN (OSS-RBA, CORENET X, eBPLS) set the agenda, so local agencies wait for central integration rather than buy independently.
Vendor evergreen maintenance models (e.g., Tyler includes upgrades in maintenance) lower the pressure to switch.

name: Government tax administration
systems: IRS Individual Master File (IMF) and Business Master File (BMF): IBM-built 1960s mainframe, COBOL and Assembly (US)
IRS CADE 2 (replacement program for IMF, in build since 2010)
FAST Enterprises GenTax (COTS integrated tax system, 60+ agencies, US states and abroad)
SAP ECC 6.0 based tax platforms, e.g. HMRC Enterprise Tax Management Platform (ETMP), 45+ tax regimes (UK)
ATO National Taxpayer System (NTS, 1975) and ATO Integrated System (AIS, 1994), partly replaced by Accenture-built Integrated Core Processing (ICP) (AU)
DJP SIDJP (Indonesia core tax system in use since 2002), replaced by Coretax (LG CNS-Qualysoft)
India Income Tax e-filing and Centralised Processing Centre (CPC 1.0, then CPC 2.0 by Infosys)
Vietnam GDT TMS centralized tax management application (rolled out 2014-2015, replaced 16 distributed apps)
Singapore IRAS IRIN (Inland Revenue Interactive Network) integrated system
In-house mainframe systems at state revenue departments and local property/council tax billing systems
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Tax administration is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software at the national level in the US, UK and AU. Each agency is a single sovereign buyer that cannot interrupt revenue collection, and it carries decades of annually amended tax law encoded in COBOL. It is less locked in SEA, where Vietnam, Indonesia and India replaced their cores between 2014 and 2025.

s1.why: Primary government sources cover the largest installed cores in several in-scope countries. GAO-25-107795 lists two Treasury tax processing systems aged 59 and 51 years, both on COBOL and Assembly. CRS IF12525 dates the IRS IMF to the 1960s. IGT/ANAO date ATO NTS to 1975 and AIS to 1994. The NAO (via The Register) reports 124 HMRC legacy systems still running in March 2024, some over 30 years old. The common replacements are also pre-cloud and on-prem in origin: FAST GenTax was built as late-1990s client-server and SAP ECC 6.0 is from 2006. Caveat: the SEA cores are newer (Vietnam TMS 2014-15, Indonesia Coretax 2025, India CPC 2.0 from 2019), so the sign holds at US/UK/AU national level and much less in VN/ID/IN.

s2.why: Several jurisdictions have primary, quantified timelines. IRS CADE 2 started in 2010 and targets FY2028, after CADE 1 was abandoned in 2009, and IMF replacement projects were suspended in May 2024 (CRS). The ATO Change Program ran Dec 2003 to June 2010, cost A$756.7m and left BAS and SG undelivered (IGT). HMRC's SAP S/4HANA contract runs to 2035. Indonesia's Coretax took from 2018 to a Dec 2024 build and a 2026 handover. The India CPC 2.0 8.5-year term comes only from search snippets and does not count.

s3.why: The only quantified evidence is from one agency. The National Taxpayer Advocate says IRS staff key in paper returns digit by digit, with transcription errors on about 22% of them and a backlog near 15M returns in 2022. That is mainly a paper-intake gap, not a spreadsheet or screen-scraping workaround for core-system limits. The ATO data synchronisation claim comes from a search summary and was not opened. Nothing was found for HMRC, the EU, or the SEA agencies.

s4.why: GAO says the two Treasury tax systems run on COBOL and Assembly, which have a dwindling pool of skilled people. The line about paying a premium for contractors is GAO's general statement across agencies, not one specific to tax. The $754m a year in the earlier research is wrong: it covers all 11 federal legacy systems. There is no quantified evidence of a skills shortage for the dominant non-US platforms (GenTax, SAP ECC, ICP, TMS, Coretax), and SAP/GenTax skills are not notably scarce. This rests on one agency's evidence.

reasons_to_stay: Failed or troubled replacements make agencies cautious: IRS CADE 1 was abandoned in 2009 after cost overruns, the ATO's 2010 ICP rollout caused processing problems and left BAS and SG on legacy, and Indonesia's Coretax drew taxpayer complaints at its 2025 launch.
Revenue continuity: the systems collect a large share of government revenue (HMRC ETMP handles about GBP 800bn a year), so cutover risk is political.
Tax law changes every year, and decades of encoded rules in COBOL/Assembly are hard to extract and re-validate.
Funding is lumpy and political: IRS IRA modernization money may run out by FY2026 and IMF replacement projects were suspended in 2024.
Procurement and sovereignty constraints: long tenders, single-source awards (SAP's GBP 275m HMRC award), and sovereign-cloud and security accreditation needs.
Incumbent integrator and COTS lock-in: Aspire-era contracts, GenTax configuration, and maintenance contracts after go-live (LG CNS kept maintenance after the Coretax handover).

DXC Assure Claims, formerly CSC / DXC RISKMASTER (corporate risk, self-insured, TPA claims)
FINEOS Claims / AdminSuite (life, accident, health, group and absence claims; company founded 1993)
Duck Creek Claims
Sapiens claims products (IDIT, ClaimsPro / ClaimsMaster)

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Claims is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Systems hold open reserves, litigation files and regulator-mandated history that must be migrated intact, and they connect to policy, payments, reinsurance and fraud tools. Unlike policy admin, though, claims is often the first core module carriers replace, and AI overlays (fraud, triage, damage estimation) can sit on top of the incumbent without replacing it.

s1.why: Primary sources date the dominant installed claims systems to before 2005, all on-prem. Guidewire's 2011 S-1 says P&C carriers run core systems often 20+ years old on outdated languages. Guidewire first sold ClaimCenter, now the most widely installed packaged claims system (270+ customers), in 2003 as on-prem Java software. RISKMASTER dates from the early 1980s and FINEOS was founded in 1993. Datos Insights (Apr 2025) quantifies it: over 50% of insurers still manage claims on legacy platforms. Two caveats. The Datos figure covers life, annuity and benefits only. The S-1 is a vendor describing the systems it wants to replace.

s2.why: Two vendors say this in their own SEC filings. Guidewire's FY2025 10-K puts initial subscription terms at usually five years, with some of seven years or longer, and calls sales cycles lengthy. Its S-1 says implementation runs 6 to 24+ months. Sapiens' FY2024 20-F says sales cycles run 1 to 2 years and delivery takes from several months to a few years. Taken together, a carrier commits to the system for several years from evaluation to go-live and beyond. The strict 7+ year contract term applies only to some Guidewire deals, so the grade rests on multi-year replacement rather than on contract length.

s3.why: The only primary source is Lloyd's Blueprint Two, which documents re-keying, manual extraction and spreadsheet bordereaux. It covers London market delegated-authority and bureau claims data, not the carrier claims systems that dominate the category. The 72% Excel/homegrown statistic comes from an industry report with no named author, relayed by ClaimsPages. No quantified source shows screen-scraping or re-keying around ClaimCenter or mainframe claims cores across carriers in general.

s4.why: Guidewire's 2011 S-1 says retiring staff are hard to replace. That is a vendor claim from 15 years ago about the systems it sells against. The Rocket Software survey (52% struggle to find legacy-skilled staff, 35% say they have adequate skills) covered 276 IT leaders across industries. It is not insurance-specific, and the article only adds insurance context in commentary. No claims-specific or insurer-specific quantified skills data exists. For ClaimCenter/Gosu, the dominant installed system, the evidence points to a large Guidewire SI talent pool, mostly in India, more than to scarcity.

reasons_to_stay: Long contracts: Guidewire initial terms run five years with annual renewals, and some run seven years or longer, which locks in the incumbent.
Implementation risk and time: 6 to 24+ months per Guidewire's S-1 and 'several months to a few years' per Sapiens. Claims history must be migrated (for example, Heritage converted about 240k claims).
Claims systems link to policy admin, payments, reserving, reinsurance, fraud tools and regulator reporting, so a swap touches many integrations.
Regulatory and audit continuity: claims reserves, litigation files and regulator-mandated data (for example, Lloyd's ECF and bureau messaging) must stay intact.
Sunk configuration: decades of customer-specific business rules live in the incumbent system.
Vendors offer an upgrade path instead of replacement (Guidewire Cloud, DXC AWS hosting), so carriers modernise in place.
High retention signals inertia (DXC cites 98.5%+ customer retention).

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category because life and annuity policies stay in force for decades. Insurers have to keep servicing closed books on the original mainframe or AS/400 PAS, and many run several PAS at once. P&C is the exception: Tier-1 carriers there have largely moved to post-2005 cores such as Guidewire and Duck Creek.

s1.why: Deloitte's Dec 2022 survey of 100 L&A CIOs found two-thirds run more than one PAS and 23% run more than four. 43% say they will not retire any legacy core system once modernization is done (77% in the smallest revenue band). Deloitte also says many life insurers still run mainframe-based legacy cores. Product histories support this: DXC PMS/Series II dates from the 1970s on z/OS, CyberLife from 1995 on z/OS, and the SMART400/LifeAsia/POLISY family runs on AS/400 (Celent says it is still in use). Caveat: the quantified evidence covers life and annuity. In US/UK Tier-1 P&C, Guidewire PolicyCenter (2006) and Duck Creek have replaced much of the pre-2005 base, so the sign is weaker for P&C. The 68% 'legacy PAS' figure in search results comes from a market-research mill and should not be cited.

s2.why: Primary filings from the main replacement vendors show this directly. Guidewire's FY2025 10-K says initial subscription terms are generally five years, some seven years or longer, with extensive evaluation cycles. Majesco's 2019 10-K cites multi-year agreements of 5-7 years. Sapiens' 2024 20-F gives a 1-2 year sales cycle and delivery of months to years. Deloitte's L&A survey describes a 'multiyear time horizon' to implement. One DXC conversion of 17 source systems took 3 years (a single case study).

s3.why: The only cited evidence is vendor marketing from Pace, an AI-agent startup. It says its agents drive green-screen and legacy admin systems, and claims about 90% task resolution at one customer (Palomar). That is one vendor and anecdotal. The McKinsey rekeying figure was never opened, and Accenture-style underwriter-time figures cover underwriting, not policy admin. Re-keying across multiple PAS is plausible given that two-thirds of L&A carriers run more than one PAS (Deloitte), but no source quantifies spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping against policy admin systems.

s4.why: The Rocket Software survey (n=276: 52% find legacy skills hard to hire, 35% say they have adequate skills) covers IT leaders at large enterprises in all industries, not insurers. Deloitte's L&A piece says only that legacy mainframe staff 'may be retired or retiring'. Celent makes the same point qualitatively. The LifeAsia/AS400 evidence is training-vendor copy and a few Kuala Lumpur job ads. No quantified, insurance-specific source shows a shortage of PAS skills.

reasons_to_stay: Reliability and stability for mission-critical processing. Celent cites this as why SMART400/Polisy/400/Life/400 remain in use.
The need to keep ongoing business running during change (Celent).
Replacement cost and risk: sales cycles of 1-2 years and delivery of months to years (Sapiens 20-F). Subscriptions run 5-7+ years (Guidewire 10-K, Majesco 10-K).
Data conversion complexity: one DXC migration moved 719,000 policy records from 17 source systems, some up to 40 years old, over 3 years.
Long-tail closed books: life and annuity policies stay in force for decades, so old products must keep being serviced.
Tightly coupled surrounding applications. A MassMutual executive cited apps tightly coupled to DXC platforms as an enabler for rehosting rather than replacing.

Regulatory reporting and actuarial logic embedded in legacy code, with outsourced AMS contracts. DXC has run application outsourcing for a VANTAGE-ONE annuity block for about 20 years (search snippet).

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: LIS is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Every change has to be revalidated under CLIA, CAP or ISO 15189, blood-bank modules are FDA-regulated devices, and decades of analyzer interfaces build up. In US hospitals, though, the systems are being replaced faster than in most legacy categories, because LIS moves with the EHR into Epic Beaker.

s1.why: In the CAP TODAY Nov 2020 LIS guide, several vendors report their own first installation dates. Together they cover most of the installed base. TECHNIDATA 1973, Sunquest 1979 (the Clinisys history page says the first lab install was 1981), Cerner PathNet 1982, SCC SoftLab 1985, Evident 1986, Orchard Harvest 1993. These run on InterSystems Cache/MUMPS or on Oracle over AIX, HP-UX or VMS, all on-prem client-server or midrange. UK WinPath (1992) and Telepath (1980s/1990s) and Australia's Auslab (c.1996) fit the same pattern. One caveat: Epic Beaker is the fastest-growing US hospital LIS and is a newer module (late 2000s). It does sit on Epic's pre-2005 Chronicles/Cache core, so the sign holds across the category.

s2.why: The UK competition regulator states it directly in its Roper/CliniSys decision (para 50): NHS LIMS contracts 'typically run for between five and ten years, often with options for extension'. That is a regulator finding for a whole national market, not one vendor. Queensland Health is a concrete case of a multi-year replacement. It awarded a 10-year, $64m Sunquest project in Feb 2018 to replace Auslab. It spent $37.5m, cancelled in 2020 after quality delays, and extended support for the 1990s-era Auslab from 2020 to 2029 (itnews). One limit: 5 to 10 years only partly meets the 7+ year threshold. The 13-year Kent and Medway figure rests on unopened search snippets.

s3.why: Re-keying is documented, but the evidence is narrow and anecdotal. JAMIA (2019) found a 3.7% transcription error rate when staff re-keyed point-of-care glucose results into the EHR. That study covered 60 clinics at two centres, and the gap sits at the device and EHR boundary, not inside the core LIS. In CAP TODAY (Nov 2022), Henry Ford's lab IT head says molecular results are still typed into the LIS by hand. No cross-lab survey quantifies spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds around the dominant LIS products.

s4.why: This is plausible but not shown for these systems specifically. Sunquest and Epic run on InterSystems Cache/MUMPS, and SCC and Cerner run on AIX/VMS/HP-UX, which are niche stacks. The only staffing evidence is general. In CAP TODAY (Nov 2022), vendors say one large institution has 110+ critical IT vacancies and that lab personnel shortages limit LIS implementation. The widely cited 20-25k shortfall is for bench technologists, not LIS analysts. No primary source (GAO, a workforce survey, or job-market data) shows that Sunquest, SoftLab, PathNet or WinPath skills are scarce. The GAO pages checked earlier mention COBOL, not MUMPS.

reasons_to_stay: Regulated validation: every LIS change must be revalidated under CLIA/CAP/ISO 15189, so switching costs are high
Deep instrument and middleware interfaces (analyzers, blood bank, microbiology) built up over decades
Tight coupling to the EHR: Epic Beaker and Cerner PathNet come bundled with the hospital EHR contract
Failed replacements: Queensland Health spent $37.5m on a Sunquest replacement, cancelled it, and kept Auslab to 2029
Long contracts: NHS LIMS contracts run 5-10 years with extensions, and network-wide programmes run up to 13 years
Decades of historical results must be migrated (Auslab held 17 years and 4 billion+ result sets per search snippet)
Blood bank modules are FDA-regulated medical devices (e.g. Sunquest device recalls), which raises the replacement bar
