reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The register carries a state guarantee of title and is bound to local land law. That makes it more locked in than typical enterprise software: replacements need statutory change, decades-long concessions and bulk data migration. But the cores are mostly bespoke systems from around 2000 rather than COBOL, so the skills risk is lower than in banking or tax.

s1.why: Primary sources show that the main register in most in-scope jurisdictions was built before 2005 as an on-prem or mainframe system and is still running. Queensland's ATS went live in 1994 and the 2026 Titles QLD practice manual still describes it. Singapore's INLIS dates from 1998. Malaysia's SPTB was implemented from 1995 and e-Tanah has replaced it in only 10 states. Karnataka's Bhoomi dates from 1999-2001. HMLR's own blog says its register and 140M documents sit on the mainframe. Landgate's CEO said all 37 Torrens jurisdictions ran old systems built around 2000. Caveats: the US county market is split, with Kofile and Tyler hosted systems spreading and AS/400 county systems shown only by anecdote, and no source gives a core build year for Indonesia's KKP.

s2.why: Primary government sources show both very long contracts and multi-year replacements. Victoria signed a 40-year registry concession in 2018 (A$2.86bn) and NSW signed a 35-year concession from 2017. Malaysia announced e-Tanah in 2003 and now targets full Peninsular coverage only by 2030. HMLR's Local Land Charges migration has slipped to end-2028, and it started its transformation in 2018 knowing it would run legacy systems for years. The Philippines LTCP was awarded in 2000 and had not started 5 years later. The concessions cover running the registry, not only software, but they still lock in the platform for decades.

s3.why: There are workarounds, but each source covers only one registry or comes from a vendor. HMLR's Strategy 2025+ says most of its data is paper, scans or PDFs, and that spatial and text data sit in unconnected systems. A UiPath case study (vendor source) says HMLR used 10 RPA bots as a tactical bridge over legacy systems. Kofile, also a vendor source, describes US county staff hand-indexing documents and searching microfiche. Landeed's business is pulling together fragmented state portals in India. No source quantifies spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping across the main registry systems.

s4.why: No source ties a skills shortage to land registry systems. HMLR does not disclose the language its mainframe uses. The only support is general COBOL statistics (Route Fifty, 2023) and an unverified Erie County, PA AS/400 anecdote whose page did not open. Many registry cores are bespoke Java or .NET systems built around 2000, and those skills are not scarce. Searches for registry-specific skills scarcity found nothing.

reasons_to_stay: The register carries a state guarantee of title (for example, the NSW Torrens Assurance Fund), so integrity outranks speed. HMLR said this explicitly when it delayed LLC to 2028.
Long concession and BOO contracts (35-40 years in AU, BOO in PH) lock in the operator's platform.
Data migration is hard: paper, microfiche and scanned titles (25M in PH, 27M titles at HMLR) must be converted while transactions keep flowing.
Changing the register often needs a statutory amendment (Malaysia amended the National Land Code for SPTB; Queensland's Land Title Act 1994 created ATS).
Procurement is political and slow, with audit-body challenges (e.g. COA questions on the PH LTCP).
Systems are bespoke to local law. Landgate found no off-the-shelf product among about 37 Torrens jurisdictions.

systems: ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP mortgage servicing system: z/OS mainframe, COBOL batch and CICS
ICE Encompass (formerly Ellie Mae) mortgage loan origination system
Finastra Loan IQ (formerly IQ Financial Systems / Misys) commercial and syndicated loan servicing
FIS Commercial Loan Servicing (formerly ACBS) commercial loan system
Sagent LoanServ (formerly Fiserv Lending Solutions) mortgage and consumer loan servicing
Nucleus Software FinnOne / FinnOne Neo retail and SME lending (APAC, India)
Loan modules in core banking systems from FIS, Fiserv, Jack Henry and CSI (US community banks)

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is more legacy-locked than typical in US mortgage servicing, where one 1960s-era mainframe (MSP) holds 63% of first-lien loans with 5 to 7 year contracts. It is less locked in origination, where Encompass and newer LOS and lending platforms are already cloud-hosted and challengers (nCino, Lentra, Mambu) are winning share.

s1.why: The dominant US servicing core is a pre-2005 mainframe, and primary sources quantify it. Black Knight's FY2022 10-K puts MSP on 32.8M first-lien loans, 63% of the US market. PennyMac's SEC-filed complaint says MSP was 'first developed over 50 years ago' and runs on a mainframe with batch processing. ICE job posts confirm z/OS COBOL/CICS. Other dominant cores also predate 2005: Loan IQ (1990s, about 70% of syndicated loan volume by vendor claim), ACBS (early 1990s) and Encompass (client-server, early 2000s). Caveats: the complaint is a litigant's allegation, and the origination side (Encompass, and FinnOne rebuilt as Neo) is now cloud-hosted. The strength rests on servicing.

s2.why: The 10-K says contracts 'typically span five to seven years', below the 7+ threshold. Deferred conversion costs amortized over 5 to 10 years point to stickiness but do not measure replacement time. The FTC 2023 ICE/Black Knight complaint (para 129) calls LOS switching 'expensive, lengthy, and resource-intensive' but gives no duration. The figure is redacted. The multi-year replacements cited are single-firm cases: PennyMac's MSP replacement ran about 2011 to 2019 (its own complaint), and Newrez's move to Valon only starts in 2027. Lock-in is real, but no primary source quantifies multi-year replacement across the installed base.

s3.why: The evidence is anecdotal or about single firms. The CFPB's 2017 Ocwen suit alleges manual workarounds on an in-house platform (REALServicing), not a dominant vendor system. PennyMac says it built 150+ custom modules around MSP's functional gaps, but those are add-on software, not spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds, and the claim comes from a litigant. The only survey (Kani 2025 via kennek, 56% manual spreadsheet reconciliation) is secondary, UK-only and about reconciliation, not origination or servicing. No primary quantified source shows spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping on the dominant systems.

s4.why: The evidence is one vendor's job posts plus a generic mainframe statistic. ICE is hiring for MSP and requires 8+ years of z/OS COBOL/CICS, which shows the skill is needed but not that it is scarce. The 71% figure for understaffed mainframe teams (BizTech 2025) is a secondary, cross-industry survey, not specific to this category. Loan IQ, Encompass and FinnOne skills are niche but not shown to be scarce. Encompass administrators are common in US mortgage hiring.

reasons_to_stay: Contracts typically run 5 to 7 years, and conversion costs are amortized over 5 to 10 years (Black Knight FY2022 10-K)
Switching is 'a significant undertaking' with lengthy timelines. ICE itself estimated the first-year cost of switching LOS for a lender (FTC complaint).
Investor and regulator reporting (GSEs, Ginnie Mae, CFPB servicing rules) is already built into incumbent systems. A rebuild risks compliance errors, as the CFPB's Ocwen case shows.
Ecosystem lock-in: ancillary services (PPE, default, data) are integrated with the incumbent LOS or servicing system, and the FTC says assembling them is a barrier to entry
Network effects in syndicated lending: agent banks and the counterparties they serve are all on Loan IQ
Data conversion risk for millions of borrower accounts. Ocwen still had 15% of a ResCap transfer unverified 3 years later.
Big-bank migrations are multi-year programs (PennyMac 2011 to 2019; Newrez to Valon starting in 2027)

name: Custom COBOL and mainframe applications (cross-industry)
systems: IBM Z mainframes running z/OS (MVS lineage) with custom COBOL, PL/I and Assembler applications
IBM CICS Transaction Server (online transaction processing, released 1969)
IBM IMS (hierarchical DB/transaction manager, installed 1968)
IBM Db2 for z/OS and VSAM data files
JCL batch and 3270 'green screen' (TN3270) terminal front ends
Micro Focus (now Rocket Software) COBOL / Enterprise Server
Unisys ClearPath Forward (MCP, from Burroughs 1961; OS 2200)
Fujitsu mainframes (sales end FY2030, support end FY2035)
Broadcom (ex-CA Technologies) mainframe tooling (IDMS, Datacom, Endevor etc.)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category: the dominant stack (z/OS, CICS, IMS, COBOL) dates from the 1960s and holds decades of undocumented business rules, and the vendor still ships new hardware every year, so staying put is cheaper and less risky than migrating.

s1.why: The dominant installed stack is IBM Z running z/OS, CICS (released 1969), IMS (installed 1968) and Enterprise COBOL. Unisys MCP dates from 1961. GAO-25-107795, a primary audit, finds that the 11 most critical US federal legacy systems are 23 to 60 years old. Two Treasury systems among them run on COBOL and Assembly. This sign holds by definition for the category, and IBM's 2022 share-of-top-50-banks figures show the base is still in use.

s2.why: GAO's primary audit is quantified. Of 10 critical federal modernizations flagged in 2019, only 3 were done by Feb 2025. Two of the rest are 5 or more years out, one has no date, and HHS plans run to FY2035. Two of the 11 systems in the 2025 review had no modernization plan at all. The evidence is strongest for government. The private-sector proof is the CBA core replacement (about 5 years, over A$1B), which is one case. It stays strong because the GAO figures span several agencies, but it is close to the line for banks.

s3.why: The only non-vendor evidence is from the Bipartisan Policy Center, a think tank. It interviewed state officials about COBOL unemployment-insurance systems and found paper processes and manual data entry. That covers one government niche, not the dominant bank, insurer and telco base. Screen-scraping of 3270 terminals is real and common, but the evidence comes from RPA vendors (UiPath terminal activities). GAO-25-107795 does not document spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds. No quantified cross-industry source was found.

s4.why: GAO (primary, 2025) says Treasury's COBOL and Assembly systems depend on languages with 'a dwindling number of people available'. It also says agencies pay a premium for specialized staff. Industry surveys add numbers, though most are vendor-commissioned. A 2018 Forrester study found enterprises lost 23% of mainframe staff in 5 years and 63% of those roles stayed unfilled. A Micro Focus survey found 60% of COBOL users name hiring as their top challenge. A 2025 survey found 71% of mainframe teams understaffed. One caveat: scarcity is weaker in IN and PH, where offshore service firms (TCS, Infosys) train mainframe staff at scale.

reasons_to_stay: Proven reliability and throughput: IBM says z17 handles up to 24 trillion operations per second and mainframes process 87% of transactions (IBM Think).
Long, costly, risky rewrites. CBA's core replacement took 5 years and cost over A$1B. GAO warns that undocumented modernization plans raise the odds of cost overruns and project failure.
Business rules are embedded in undocumented code that nobody fully understands.
Gartner (cited by IBM) expects 75% of 'mainframe exit' vendors to pivot or exit by 2030, which makes exit look risky.
Vendors commit to long roadmaps: Unisys ClearPath Forward 2050 and IBM's annual z cycles.
Regulatory and operational risk of migrating core ledgers, payments and tax systems.

Oracle Health (Cerner) Patient Accounting, Soarian Financials and Invision (ex-Siemens/SMS), being folded into RevElate
MEDITECH MAGIC (1982) and Client/Server (1994) financials, migrating to Expanse
TruBridge (ex-CPSI, Healthland) community-hospital EHR and RCM
Altera Digital Health Paragon and Sunrise (ex-Allscripts/Eclipsys)
SAP IS-H patient management and billing (DACH and EU hospitals; mainstream support ends 2027, extended support to 2030)
InterSystems TrakCare (Asia/Oceania, UK, Middle East)
HBCIS patient administration system (Queensland Health, early 1980s) and DXC iPM/webPAS (Australia)
VA VistA (US government, being replaced by Oracle Health)
Indonesia SIMRS (hospital information systems) plus BPJS V-Claim/E-Klaim INA-CBG, often not bridged to each other
Singapore National Billing System (NBS) alongside the Epic-based NGEMR
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital RCM is more locked in than typical enterprise software because billing shares one M-based database with the EHR, so replacing billing means replacing the EHR. But the dominant cores are still actively developed, and most of the manual pain comes from payer connectivity, not the cores' age.

s1.why: The installed base is measured and old. KLAS market share (via HealthSystemCIO, May 2026) puts Epic at 43.7% of US acute hospitals, Oracle Health/Cerner at 21.9% and MEDITECH at 14.7%, about 80% of US hospitals combined. All three cores shipped well before 2005 as on-prem or client-server systems: Epic Resolute in 1987 on Chronicles/M, MEDITECH MAGIC in 1982 and Client/Server in 1994 (Expanse only in 2018), and Cerner Millennium, Soarian and Invision in the 1980s to 2000s. Outside the US the picture is the same: SAP IS-H has run for over 30 years, HBCIS dates from the 1980s, and TrakCare sits on an M database. Caveats: the dates come from Wikipedia and FundingUniverse company histories, not vendor filings. Epic is actively developed and often hosted. Physician-practice billing (athenahealth, eClinicalWorks) is mostly cloud, so this grade applies to hospital RCM.

s2.why: The evidence is a set of public-sector cases, not a category-wide measure. NYC H+H spent $289M over five years on Epic revenue cycle (a Politico reprint). iTnews estimates about seven years to replace Queensland's HBCIS. DSAG says tendering an IS-H successor alone takes about two years. The VA's 10-year Oracle Cerner contract and the LA County and SF 10-year Epic contracts were seen only in search snippets or on blocked pages. No KLAS or survey data on implementation length or typical contract term was found. Replacement also usually means a full EHR replacement, so these timelines describe EHR programs more than billing alone. The sign is plausible and repeated, but anecdotal.

s3.why: The 2024 CAQH Index is a primary, industry-wide, quantified source. Only 35% of medical prior authorizations are fully electronic (X12 278). 39% go through web portals or IVR, which means re-keying, and 22% are fully manual (phone, fax, mail, email). CAQH sizes the remaining savings at about $20B. RCM is also a main market for RPA bots that scrape payer portals. Caveat: the re-keying is driven mostly by payer-side connectivity, not by the age of the provider's billing core. The UC Davis 'dummy appointment' workaround is one anecdote, and the Indonesian SIMRS/E-Klaim re-entry claim comes from a vendor blog.

s4.why: The only cited source is a trade opinion piece (Health IT Outcomes) calling MUMPS programmers a dying breed. It has no labor-market data. Epic skills are scarce mainly because Epic gates certification behind employer sponsorship, not because the skill base is shrinking. Billing analyst roles themselves are configuration work, not M coding. No source quantifies an SAP IS-H/ABAP skills shortage. Surveys do report RCM staffing shortages (for example 63% of providers), but those are about coders and billers, not skills for a legacy system. The sign is plausible but not shown.

reasons_to_stay: Billing is tied into the EHR. Epic Resolute and MEDITECH financials share one database with scheduling and clinical data, so replacing billing usually means replacing the EHR.
Cash-flow risk at go-live. After the UC Davis Epic conversion, staff resorted to 'dummy' appointments to keep certain billing running.
Very high cost and long timelines: $289M over five years for NYC H+H revenue cycle, about 7 years and $200M+ for Queensland's PAS replacement.
Payer and regulatory rules are encoded over decades (US payer edits, German DRG billing in IS-H, BPJS INA-CBG, PhilHealth case rates). Rebuilding them is risky.
Vendors keep extending support. SAP IS-H has extended maintenance to 2030 and a transition option to 2033. Queensland bought extended HBCIS support to 2023.
Procurement friction. DSAG estimates two years just to tender an IS-H successor, and public buyers must run formal tenders.
Incumbent consolidation keeps customers in place. Oracle is folding Soarian and Invision into RevElate, IKS Health bought TruBridge, and MEDITECH reports 84% legacy retention.

name: Mortgage servicing
systems: ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP Mortgage Servicing Platform: z/OS mainframe, COBOL batch + CICS, DB2/VSAM, vendor-hosted
Sagent LoanServ (ex-Fiserv MortgageServ), now marketed as the Dara cloud platform
FICS Mortgage Servicer (on-prem / hosted, for mid-size banks, credit unions and commercial servicers)
Phoebus Software platform (UK/Ireland mortgage and savings administration, designed 1989)
Target Group (Tech Mahindra) loan management / servicing platform (UK)
Nucleus Software FinnOne / FinnOne Neo lending suite (India, SE Asia)
Core-banking loan modules (Temenos, Finacle, Silverlake and similar) used for mortgage servicing at Asian banks. Inferred, no source found for this study.
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Mortgage servicing is more legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category because one vendor-hosted COBOL/CICS mainframe system (ICE MSP) runs roughly half or more of US mortgage loans, and network effects across subservicers, MSR transfers and GSE reporting make leaving costly. That lock-in is mostly a US phenomenon: elsewhere servicing sits inside general core-banking or lending suites.

s1.why: The dominant US system is ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP. Black Knight's FY2022 10-K, a primary and quantified source, puts it at about 36M active loans against a US market of about 66M first and second liens and lines of credit. ICE's own 2026 MSP job post asks for z/OS COBOL batch, CICS, JCL and DB2/VSAM, which confirms the mainframe stack independently of PennyMac's partisan '50-year-old mainframe' claim. The 10-K itself only calls MSP 'a SaaS solution' and does not describe the technology. Outside the US the evidence is weak: Phoebus (UK, 1989) has no share data, and no specific pre-2005 servicing core was tied to the SE Asian regions. The strong grade rests on US dominance only.

s2.why: The evidence does not meet the 7+ year or multi-year bar for the dominant system. The FY2019 10-K figure is '12 to 18 months, or longer' to switch, which is not multi-year, and the FY2022 10-K only says 'long-term contracts' with no length. Published MSP renewals are 5 years (Cenlar, EverBank). The one 7-year term found is Mr. Cooper's commitment to Sagent, a single deal reported in trade press. A 7-year LoanCare renewal on MSP appeared in search results but was not verified. PennyMac's multi-year, module-by-module exit is one partisan case. The lock-in is real (30-year client tenures such as Cenlar), but neither duration test is shown directly.

s3.why: The evidence is indirect, and the main source is a litigant. PennyMac says it built 'hundreds' of bolt-on modules around MSP and that data is downloaded from and uploaded back to MSP. CFPB Supervisory Highlights Issue 11 (2016) found IT staff manually overriding data fields during servicing transfers, which is a transfer-specific finding. No primary or quantified source shows spreadsheets, re-keying or screen-scraping as routine practice across MSP or other servicing users.

s4.why: The only evidence specific to this category is one ICE job post for the MSP team. It asks for 8+ years of z/OS COBOL/CICS and treats AI coding tools as a plus, which suggests scarcity but does not quantify it. The Deloitte survey cited by BizTech (71% of firms say mainframe teams are understaffed) covers financial services in general, not mortgage servicing. No mortgage-specific vacancy, wage or retirement data was found.

reasons_to_stay: Switching takes 12 to 18 months or longer, and the cost is significant (Black Knight FY2019 10-K).
Regulators expect extensive testing and validation before a servicer changes major systems (PennyMac complaint).
Servicing transfers carry CFPB exposure: lost loss-mitigation documents and late payment crediting during data moves.
Investor, GSE and agency reporting (Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie, FHA/VA) is already built and certified on the incumbent.
Multi-year contracts (for example Mr. Cooper's 7-year commitment to Sagent) and long renewals lock buyers in.
Network effects: subservicers, MSR buyers and vendors integrate to MSP formats, so leaving it adds friction on every transfer.
Vendor litigation risk: Black Knight sued PennyMac in 2019 when it left MSP.

name: Payroll and HR administration
systems: SAP ERP HCM / SAP HR & Payroll (R/3, ECC 6.0), with country payroll versions
Oracle PeopleSoft HCM (HRMS)
Oracle E-Business Suite HRMS / Payroll (e.g. NHS ESR)
Infor Lawson S3 HR/Payroll (ex-Lawson Software)
UKG (Kronos) Workforce Central time and attendance, on-prem
ADP legacy in-country and global payroll platforms (ADP iHCM, ADP Global Payroll), being moved to ADP Lyric / Workforce Now
In-house COBOL mainframe government payroll (e.g. California Uniform State Payroll System, Colorado CPPS)
IBM AS/400 (IBM i) payroll applications at municipalities and mid-market firms
Spreadsheet-based payroll (Excel) at SMBs
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Payroll is more locked-in than typical enterprise software at the deep end: statutory tax, award and union rules are hard-coded, errors are not tolerated, and the evidence shows multi-year, billion-dollar public-sector replacements. It is less locked-in at the top and the bottom, where Workday (65%+ of the Fortune 500) and SaaS bureaus such as ADP RUN and Gusto already hold much of the installed base.

s1.why: First-ship dates are solid. SAP R/3 HR shipped in 1992, PeopleSoft HRMS in 1989, Lawson started as mainframe software, and California's payroll is a mainframe set of 12 systems, some nearly 50 years old. SAP's cloud Employee Central Payroll still runs the old SAP HCM payroll engine. But no source puts a number on the installed-base share of these cores. The one quantified share figure points the other way: Workday's 10-K says it serves 65%+ of the Fortune 500 on a core first shipped after 2005. US SMB payroll is mostly SaaS or bureau (ADP RUN, Gusto). So pre-2005 cores dominate public sector, higher education and part of mid-to-large enterprise, but not the category as a whole.

s2.why: Two separate primary, quantified cases on different stacks. (1) California LAO: the CSPS replacement costs about $1.2bn, takes about 6 years and completes Sept 2031. It follows the 21st Century/MyCalPAYS attempt, which began in 2004 and was suspended in 2013 after nearly a decade. (2) NHS England and Wales: the Oracle EBS-based ESR, which pays 1.9m staff, moves to a 15-year, GBP 1.4bn (inc. VAT) Infosys contract, and ESR support runs to 2035. SAP HCM extended maintenance to 2030 and H4S4 to 2040 extend the timeline further. Caveat: the quantified evidence is all public sector. Private-enterprise replacements are usually 12-36 months.

s3.why: The primary evidence is one 2013 municipal audit (Killeen TX): paper timecards are re-keyed into an AS400 and every check is recalculated in Excel. The better quantified source is the EY-PayrollOrg Payroll Pulse Survey (2022-23): 40% use SQL-fed spreadsheets and 18% manual processes as their primary way of working with payroll data. That covers data and reporting work, not core processing, and the survey does not tie it to legacy cores. Cloud payroll users report the same habit. The 51% spreadsheet figure is a vendor-cited poll (Strada/Alight).

s4.why: The only primary evidence is California LAO Report 3590 (2017), where the State Controller reports trouble hiring mainframe staff for the payroll system covering about 260k employees. The 2025 LAO CSPS report does not repeat this. InfoWorld (2008) is secondary. Nothing shows scarce SAP HCM, PeopleSoft or Lawson skills, which make up most of the installed base, or any skills gap in APAC or India. SAP HCM consultants are still abundant, and the market is moving toward SuccessFactors ECP.

reasons_to_stay: Payroll is mission-critical and has zero tolerance for error. Queensland Health's 2010 SAP payroll go-live underpaid or failed to pay about 78,000 staff and cost about AUD 1.2bn, which makes buyers very risk-averse.
Deep local statutory logic (tax, social security, awards and union agreements, e.g. PPh 21/BPJS in Indonesia, Australian awards) is embedded and tested in the old system.
Vendors keep extending support (SAP HCM to 2030 and H4S4 to 2040; PeopleSoft rolling to at least 2036), which removes any forcing deadline.
Replacement is a reimplementation, not an upgrade (e.g. Kronos WFC to UKG Pro WFM), and needs parallel payroll runs and data migration.
Public-sector procurement cycles and long managed-service contracts (NHS ESR: 15 years) lock incumbents in.
Integration with GL, time and attendance, pensions and benefits, and banks.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More locked-in than a typical enterprise category. Decades of member benefit history and statutory rules must be migrated exactly, and many dominant buyers are single government funds, so replacement takes 5 to 15 years. Australia's super market is the exception: post-2010 platforms and frequent fund mergers make it less locked-in.

s1.why: FIS Omni/Relius is the dominant US DC recordkeeping engine (650 clients, 68m participants). The vendor's own retirement lead says it was built in COBOL more than 30 years ago and is only being rebuilt for cloud in 2026. Public plans show the same pattern in their own releases: Washington DRS was replacing a 30-year-old system in 2023, Massachusetts SRB a 38-year-old one in 2010, NY MEBEL ran on z/OS, and CalSTRS used its legacy system until 2025. Caveats: Australia's leading core (Bravura Sonata, launched 2010) is after 2005, and the UK's Altair has no disclosed first-ship date. So this is strong for the US and public sector, and less certain for AU and UK.

s2.why: Several primary agency sources each quantify a long replacement. CalSTRS's Pension Solution started pre-implementation in 2010, got budget approval in 2014 and went live in September 2025, with a $523m budget plus $105m post-go-live. Washington DRS signed a 4-year implementation plus 2 years of support with Sagitec (2023). EPFO's CITES 2.01 was approved in 2021 and went live in July 2026. FIS's own Omni rebuild took 4 years. Capita seeks 5 to 10 year TPA terms. Multi-year replacement is the norm across the dominant buyers.

s3.why: The direct evidence is vendor-authored. Sagitec's TRS case study describes re-keying across systems and employers sending data on paper or disk, and Aware Super's 'paper-based legacy systems' quote is also vendor-adjacent. UK industry material (TPR record-keeping research and PASA, both reported second-hand) says about a third of schemes keep non-digital records and that data gathering and calculations are manual. That points to paper and archive records, not quantified spreadsheet or screen-scraping workarounds on top of the dominant platforms. Plausible, but not primary or quantified.

s4.why: The main citation is a single 2013 Computerworld article about one system (NY MEBEL). The audit behind it came from NY DFS and the Comptroller disputed it. COBOL, CICS, DB2 and OmniScript skills for FIS OmniPlus appear in job and CV listings, but no source quantifies a shortage. Nothing was found for UK, AU or Asian provident funds. Dated and anecdotal.

reasons_to_stay: Benefit rules span decades of legislative changes and member history (DB accrual, tranches, transitional protections) that must be migrated exactly. HESTA moved more than a decade of data and still had a members-locked-out cutover period
Regulatory and fiduciary risk: payment errors to retirees are highly visible, and boards prefer incumbent stability
Long outsourcing and TPA contracts (Capita seeks 5 to 10 years) bundle software and administration
Challenger financial fragility: GROW Inc carried going-concern audit doubts and needed client debt and equity support before MUFG agreed to acquire it in 2026
Big-bang regulatory deadlines (Dutch Wtp by 2028, UK pensions dashboards) push funds to extend incumbents rather than switch mid-reform
Concentrated incumbent ecosystems (Heywood Altair across LGPS, FIS Omni across US recordkeepers) supply frameworks, interfaces and skilled staff
Fund mergers (AU consolidation from 1,656 to 771 APRA funds in 5 years) often settle on the acquirer's existing platform instead of a new one

name: Port and container terminal operating systems (TOS)
systems: Navis SPARCS / SPARCS Express (Kaleris), on-prem predecessor of N4
Navis N4 (Kaleris), first site live 2006
PSA CITOS (in-house, 1988)
Hutchison Ports nGen (in-house, 2003)
Tideworks Mainsail / Mainsail Vanguard (SSA Marine subsidiary)
Total Soft Bank CATOS (Korea)
RBS TOPS / TOPX (Australia)
Pelindo legacy TOS / PTOS-M being consolidated onto ILCS TOS Nusantara (Indonesia)
Operator in-house legacy TOS (for example Patrick Terminals' 30-year in-house system replaced by N4 in 2020; seen only in search snippets)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. A TOS is real-time control of cranes, gates and automated equipment, so cutovers need operational shutdowns and cores run 20 to 30 years. It is less locked than mainframe categories, because the dominant product (Navis N4, 2006) is a vendor-supported Java platform that gets regular upgrades and is moving to cloud.

s1.why: The market's dominant lineages began as on-prem client-server systems before or around 2005. PSA CITOS dates from 1988 and Navis SPARCS from 1989 (academic history). Hutchison nGen went live in 2003, RBS TOPX shipped in 1996, and Tideworks Mainsail launched in 1999. Primary customer sources confirm long-lived pre-2005 cores in production. GPA ran SPARCS/Express at Garden City from fall 2000 until its N4 cutover in April 2022. Patrick's CIO described replacing a '30-year-old legacy TOS' with N4 in 2020. Two caveats. The market leader, Navis N4 (389 terminals in GPA's FAQ, 500+ Navis ports per Kaleris), first went live in 2006, so it is a mid-2000s Java client-server rewrite rather than mainframe or midrange. No source documents mainframe or midrange architecture anywhere in this category.

s2.why: Primary operator sources show decades of tenure and multi-year replacement programmes at the largest operators. GPA ran SPARCS/Express for about 21 years (2000 to 2022). Patrick ran an in-house TOS for about 30 years. APM Terminals set a target to standardise its global portfolio on N4 by end-2021, but Aarhus only went live in March 2022, after data-migration problems that raised truck turn times. DP World Australia's consolidation of 19 systems onto N4 ran over several years. Single-site projects take 12 to 24 months, but that figure comes only from a vendor (INTECH). Contract lengths of 7+ years are not directly documented. The evidence is tenure and programme duration.

s3.why: The best quantified evidence is a global Tideworks survey with no stated sample size or year. In it, 89% of terminals use a TOS, yet 56% still rely on email and spreadsheets, only 33% use APIs, and 45%+ report integration problems with partners. That is vendor marketing, and it describes manual coordination around the TOS with partners, not re-keying or screen-scraping of the TOS itself. Portwise, a consultancy blog, says small terminals plan berths on spreadsheets or whiteboards. No independent or primary source quantifies workarounds at the large N4, CITOS or nGen sites.

s4.why: All of the scarcity evidence comes from one recruiter, KiTalent, across content-marketing pieces on Rijeka, Genoa and Sohar. They claim 8 to 11 months to hire senior N4 specialists, an N4 vacancy left open for about 11 months, and roughly 200 to 250 Navis/Kalmar automation engineers in the whole GCC. These pieces are unverified and possibly templated. The scarcity they describe is vendor-specific configuration know-how for a current product (N4, Java/Groovy), not a dying language or platform. No APAC, US or independent labour-market data was found.

reasons_to_stay: A TOS is mission-critical real-time control. Failed cutovers hurt operations badly: Felixstowe's June 2018 switch from Navis to Hutchison nGen caused lost boxes and truck queues of up to 16 hours (seen in search snippets; the Seatrade article returned 403).
Cutovers need a full operational shutdown window (GPA stopped operations overnight for N4) and 12 to 24 months of implementation.

Deep integration with automated equipment, gates, RFID, EDI and port community systems (PD Ports' Navis role lists SPARCS, MCP, Fast gate, WhereNet RFID, Camco Autogate, VBS). Every interface has to be re-done.
Data migration of 10+ years of container, vessel and customer history takes 4 to 8 months.
Big operators treat their in-house TOS as a competitive asset (PSA CITOS, Hutchison nGen) and build the next generation in-house rather than buy.
There is a small, concentrated vendor field, and specialist TOS staff are hard to hire. Both raise switching risk.

Oracle E-Business Suite (Oracle Applications / Financials: Purchasing, iProcurement, Payables), on-prem
JD Edwards World (RPG on IBM System/3x, AS/400 / IBM i) Accounts Payable and Procurement
JD Edwards EnterpriseOne and PeopleSoft Financials/Supply Chain (Oracle-owned on-prem)
Ariba Buyer (on-prem e-procurement, 1996-era), now SAP Ariba

Excel spreadsheets and paper/PDF invoice keying layered on top of the ERP
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software at the core, because purchasing and AP sit inside the ERP system of record (SAP ECC, Oracle EBS) and replacing them takes years. It is less locked in at the edges, because cloud P2P and AP-automation overlays bolt on easily and the clerk-level skills stay plentiful.

s1.why: The dominant enterprise purchasing and payables core is SAP ECC MM/FI-AP. Its R/3 base shipped in 1992 as three-tier client/server, and R/2 dates from 1979 on mainframe. Gartner counts about 35,000 ECC customers worldwide and finds 61% had not licensed S/4HANA by end-Q4 2024, so most of the installed base still runs the pre-2005 core. Oracle EBS (late 1980s) and JD Edwards World (RPG on AS/400) add to this, though no install counts were found for them. One caveat: mid-market and SMB AP is moving to cloud (NetSuite, QuickBooks Online, Coupa), so this grade holds for the enterprise segment only.

s2.why: In 2020 SAP moved the Business Suite 7 deadline to end-2027, with paid extended maintenance to 2030, because of 'longer conversion phases' (primary). An ISG survey of 200 large firms found nearly 60% of SAP migrations run late and over budget. Gartner/ISG figures show 61% of ECC customers had not licensed S/4 eight years after the deadline was first announced. Birmingham City Council's SAP R/3 to Oracle replacement for finance and procurement started in 2018 and was still incomplete in 2026. All of this evidence is about the ERP as a whole, not P2P specifically. Bolt-on cloud P2P tools such as Coupa deploy in months, but the system of record underneath them is still slow to replace.

s3.why: Manual invoice keying is real and quantified. Ardent's 2025 ePayables survey (n=204, vendor-sponsored by Bottomline) found 48.6% of invoices arrive non-electronically and only 35.4% go straight through. But the cause is suppliers sending paper and PDF invoices, and the survey covers AP teams on every kind of system, including modern cloud ones. It does not tie re-keying or spreadsheet workarounds to the legacy ERP cores. Birmingham's GBP 5M of manual workaround labour is a single anecdote, and it comes from the replacement system failing, not the legacy one.

s4.why: The only quantified scarcity evidence covers the IBM i/RPG slice: Fortra 2026 found 69% name IBM i skills a top concern. That slice (JD Edwards World and homegrown AS/400 AP) is a minority of the installed base. For the dominant systems, SAP ECC and Oracle EBS, ABAP, MM and FI-AP consultants and AP clerks are widely available in every region in scope. The SAP skills-shortage surveys (for example UKISUG, 63%) measure S/4HANA migration skills, not scarcity of skills to run the legacy system. Tally, MISA and Accurate skills are abundant among SMB accountants.

reasons_to_stay: The ERP is the system of record for the general ledger, vendor master and 3-way match. Ripping out purchasing/AP means touching the core ERP, and Birmingham's SAP R/3 replacement shows what that risk costs.

Vendors keep extending support: SAP maintenance runs to 2027, optional to 2030, then customer-specific. Oracle extended EBS 12.2 Premier Support repeatedly (per search results, through at least 2036/2037). That removes any forcing deadline.
Heavy customisation (ABAP, RPG, Oracle Forms) encodes approval rules, tax and local e-invoicing compliance.
Bolt-on AP automation (capture, workflow) can be layered on top without replacing the core.
SMBs in IN, ID, VN rely on local tax/e-invoice compliance built into Tally, Accurate and MISA, and accountants are trained on them.
Migration is multi-year, scarce SI capacity goes to S/4HANA conversions, and finance teams fear period-close disruption.

NCR Voyix legacy retail POS portfolio (e.g., NCR/Retalix store systems)

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is less locked in than a typical enterprise one at the till: store POS gets replaced in months on a 5 to 7 year hardware cycle, and SMBs are moving straight to cloud POS. It is more locked in at the merchandising core (RMS, MMS on IBM i, SAP IS-Retail, homegrown systems), where custom pricing and inventory logic makes replacement risky, as Lidl's failed EUR 500M project shows.

s1.why: Several separate vendor lineages at the enterprise tier date from before 2005 and run on-prem or midrange. IBM/Toshiba 4690 OS shipped in 1993, and Toshiba's own site now lists SurePOS ACE under 'Legacy Systems'. It is closed to new customers but still supported under service contracts. JDA/Blue Yonder MMS runs on IBM i and had nearly 400 accounts in 2014 (IT Jungle). Oracle RMS comes from Retek, bought in 2005, and Xstore from MICROS/Datavantage. That is several vendors, and Toshiba's own page is a primary source. Caveats: there is no current share figure (the about 12% Toshiba POS share in Wikipedia dates from 2005), and the SMB long tail is mostly on cloud POS now. Strong holds for the enterprise and grocery tier only.

s2.why: The main evidence is one anecdote: Lidl's roughly 7-year, about EUR 500M failed SAP for Retail project, which replaced a homegrown system rather than a packaged product. The 12 to 18 month Xstore implementation figure comes from a partner with a stake in the answer, and the NCR 10-K only says contracts can slow the sunset of legacy products. No source gives contract lengths of 7+ years. Some evidence points the other way: vendor case studies report store-POS replacements in under a year (Bath & Body Works, 1,925 stores; Vitamin Shoppe, 700+ stores in under 6 months). Multi-year timelines are plausible for merchandising cores (RMS, MMS, IS-Retail) but are not shown for POS lanes.

s3.why: The only quantified source is a 2014 Boston Retail Partners survey, released through a vendor (Logility) press release. It found more than 60% of respondents used spreadsheets or homegrown tools for planning. That covers merchandise planning, not the POS or merchandising system of record, and it is over 10 years old. The 2026 Incisiv/Anaplan figure on monthly rebalancing only hints at manual work. Spreadsheet-based planning around legacy merchandising systems is widely reported, but no current primary source ties it to the dominant installed systems.

s4.why: The Fortra 2026 IBM i survey (315 respondents) puts skills as the top concern for 69% of IBM i shops. That bears on JDA MMS and homegrown RPG merchandising systems, but the survey has no retail breakdown and covers only one platform. No quantified source was found for scarce 4690/ACE, Retek RMS or Xstore skills. Skills for Oracle Retail and Xstore look reasonably available through SIs, especially in India. Scarcity is plausible for 4690 and RPG but is inferred, not shown for this category.

reasons_to_stay: Checkout downtime costs revenue directly, and offline-capable lanes (e.g., SurePOS ACE offline functionality) are trusted.

Deep customization of merchandising logic. Lidl's eLWIS failed partly because SAP valued inventory at retail price while Lidl used purchase price, and Lidl reverted to its old system after about EUR 500M.
Long hardware and service contracts. 4690 is still supported under service contracts, and NCR says contracts can hinder legacy sunset.
Integration web of payments certification (EMV/PCI), loyalty, fuel and scale peripherals, and ERP batch interfaces that would all need re-testing.
Peak-season change freezes and multi-thousand-store rollout logistics stretch replacements over years.
Vendors offer in-place paths (Toshiba ELERA 'without requiring infrastructure replacement', LS Nav to LS Central, Oracle cloud upgrades) that lower switching pressure.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software in higher ed: 1980s-90s cores still run at about a third of North American institutions, and the fixed academic calendar plus regulator reporting (IPEDS, HESA, PDDikti) stretch replacement to 5+ years. It is less locked in K-12, where cloud MIS vendors took most of the English schools market within a decade.

s1.why: Quantified market data shows that the dominant North American higher-ed SIS installs are pre-2005 cores. Ellucian Banner holds 24% and Colleague 11% (ListEdTech, Jan 2025), and Jenzabar and PeopleSoft Campus Solutions (first deployed 1998-99) come next. Banner dates from the 1980s on Oracle Forms. Colleague signed its first client in 1979 and runs on a UniData multivalue stack. Tribal's FY2024 annual report covers UK HE. SITS:Vision (1991) leads that market, and only about a third of customers run it in Tribal Cloud, so about two thirds are still on-prem. One caveat is that K-12 SIS is different. PowerSchool is cloud-delivered, and English schools have largely moved off client-server SIMS (31.7% share in Oct 2025, with Arbor at 44%).

s2.why: Several primary institutional sources show multi-year programs for the dominant systems. Lehigh is running a five-year program just to move from on-prem Banner to Banner SaaS. WashU's student-system replacement was planned from 2020 and went live in stages in 2024-25, and the whole Workday program ran at least 7 years for $265M+. The Callista universities extended a legacy SMS twice, most recently with a 5-year A$55M agreement in 2021. ListEdTech also reports that Banner's growth comes from upgrades and migrations, not new implementations. The evidence is per-institution, not a category-wide survey, but it is consistent across vendors and regions.

s3.why: The only cited evidence is a trade-press article (EdTech Magazine, Mar 2026) on shadow data in higher ed. Staff export rosters and student data to spreadsheets, but the article does not tie this to Banner, Colleague, SITS or PeopleSoft and does not quantify it. The Indonesian PDDikti Feeder evidence is a SIAKAD vendor's marketing claim. No primary or quantified source shows re-keying or screen-scraping as standard practice on the dominant installed systems.

s4.why: The only primary source is one vendor. Tribal's FY2024 annual report notes that SMS customers face challenges in finding and retaining resources to manage technical debt. Colleague's multivalue stack (UniData, Envision, UniBasic) is truly niche, but that evidence comes from job-posting search snippets. Banner, the largest install base, runs on Oracle PL/SQL and Forms, and those skills are widely available. EDUCAUSE hiring-difficulty data covers higher-ed IT in general, not SIS skills.

reasons_to_stay: Replacement is a 3-7 year, high-risk program (Lehigh plans five years for Banner SaaS alone), and it has to fit around the fixed academic calendar.
Decades of local customization, regulatory reporting (IPEDS, HESA/OfS returns, DfE census, PDDikti Feeder) and financial-aid logic are embedded in the old core.
Failed implementations are costly. Tribal settled its dispute with NTU Singapore in 2024 after the SITS contract was terminated, and the settlement plus legal costs came to £3.0m.

Vendors keep extending legacy support. Oracle committed PeopleSoft support to at least 2037, and the Callista universities extended support again in 2021 even though Tribal had said in 2015 that support would last only seven years.
Incumbents offer a lift-and-shift path to vendor-hosted cloud (Banner SaaS, Tribal Cloud) that keeps the same data model and avoids a re-platform.
Integrations with LMS, CRM, finance and HR all depend on the SIS schema.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Billing is more locked in than most enterprise software: a handful of incumbents (Amdocs, CSG, Ericsson, Oracle) bill on 15- to 35-year relationships, and every failed cutover hits revenue directly. The lock-in comes from contracts and embedded tariff logic more than from scarce COBOL skills, because most cores are Oracle/C++/Java rather than mainframe.

s1.why: Primary filings show the dominant installed cores predate 2005 and were built as mainframe or on-prem client-server systems. CSG's CCS/ACP, the US cable billing platform behind Charter and Comcast (about 36% of CSG's 2025 revenue), began inside First Data in 1982. It ran on outsourced FDC mainframe capacity, moved to Infocrossing mainframe service in 2008 (10-K/A Exhibit 10.41A) and was upgraded to ACP in 2004. Amdocs' own filings date its billing software to 1982. Ericsson BSCS shipped in 1990 as client-server on Oracle, and Portal Infranet dates to the 1990s. Two caveats. Current CSG mainframe hosting was not confirmed in a recent filing. BSCS and Portal dates rest on Wikipedia. The pre-2005 origin still holds across the main vendors, not just one.

s2.why: Primary sources from more than one dominant vendor show very long contracts and multi-year replacements. TCI signed a 15-year exclusive CSG contract in 1997, and Comcast later assumed it. Two-thirds of accounts had moved to ACP by 2005, a year after the 2004 upgrade. Comcast renewed for six more years in Nov 2024, through 2030, on a 35+ year relationship. CSG's Sept 2025 8-K extended Charter from Mar 2028 to Sept 30, 2031. On the Amdocs side, Globe Telecom (PH) took a seven-year BSS transformation agreement, and vendors describe Tier-1 BSS transformations as about 3-year programmes. Several of these sources are press releases, but the CSG terms come from SEC filings.

s3.why: The only evidence is consultant and vendor commentary. Cambridge MC describes staff re-keying and reconciling between disconnected BSS. Revenue-assurance vendors such as Subex and CSG insights say operators still compare billing and network data in spreadsheets and calculate partner settlements there. No survey or primary operator source quantifies spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds on the dominant billing platforms. The PwC '3-8% revenue loss' figure appears only second-hand.

s4.why: The only telecom-specific source is an AWS blog, a vendor with a migration motive, warning that shrinking mainframe expertise threatens telco BSS knowledge. systems: China Systems Eximbills (Wang VS, then AS/400, PC LAN, DEC VAX, Java EE from 2002)

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category on the core platform. A few 1980s-1990s engines (IMEX, Trade Innovation, Eximbills) dominate, and live multi-year instruments make migration hard. But much of the manual work comes from paper trade documents and UCP rules rather than from the software, so the workaround and skills signs are weaker than the platform sign.

s1.why: The dominant back-office engines all predate 2005 and were built for on-prem or host platforms. Surecomp IMEX started on IBM CICS mainframe and was only later rehosted to Linux/Oracle Tuxedo ART. DBS chose it in the late 1990s, and Absa has used Surecomp since 1998. Finastra (Misys) Trade Innovation was built by the Kapiti/Aregon team in the 1990s and was live at Bank of the West by 2000 and at First Hawaiian by 2004. China Systems Eximbills began around 1983 on Wang VS and then ran on AS/400 and VAX. CGI Trade360 dates from about 2000 (vendor brochure), though it was hosted, not on-prem. Several vendors back this, and Finastra's and CGI's own materials give 25+ years. Caveat: the Eximbills history comes from an archived wiki, and the IMEX CICS origin comes from Oracle/Capterra secondary text.

s2.why: The evidence is a few single-bank cases, with no category-level data. HSBC picked CGI Trade360 in April 2019, and the first two markets went live in October 2022 (about 3.5 years). BNI was still migrating international locations onto Trade Innovation in 2026. Long tenures are also anecdotal: Bank of the West ran TI 2000-2008, and a 403'd snippet says one bank ran Surecomp IBSnet for 15+ years. No source gives contract lengths or a survey of replacement durations across banks.

s3.why: ICC's 2018 Global Survey (250+ banks, 90+ countries) is quantified: 52% said paper had not been removed at all from document verification, and only 9% said tech had cut time or cost. That shows paper-bound, manual checking. It does not show that users work around the software with spreadsheets, re-keying or screen-scraping. Much of the paper burden comes from the trade documents themselves (bills of lading, UCP 600 rules), not from the legacy engines. The re-keying point (staff copy OCR output into back-end fields) comes from a 2016 BCG article, which is secondary and dated. No source quantifies spreadsheet use.

s4.why: No citable evidence shows a shortage of the platform skills (CICS/COBOL for IMEX, AS/400 for old Eximbills). Only a closed Surecomp COBOL posting was seen. What is documented is a shortage of trade-operations domain expertise. ITFA (May 2025) says 26% of trade professionals are near retirement, and it projects a 43% drop in qualified practitioners by 2030, but gives no underlying source. GTR quotes recruiters who see the same small candidate pool. That is a secondary source about the domain, not about the system. It is weak, bordering on not_met.

reasons_to_stay: In-flight instruments: LCs, standbys and guarantees can run for years, so live books have to be migrated in the middle of their life. The BNI migration was still moving nine international locations in 2026.
SWIFT MT/ISO 20022 certification and UCP 600/URDG rule handling are built into the incumbents (IMEX is fully SWIFT certified).
Deep integration with core banking, accounting, AML/sanctions screening, treasury and limits. The vendor factsheet lists all of these integrations.
Volume is concentrated in a few large banks, so smaller banks see little ROI in replacing a working system.
Incumbents keep releasing new versions (IMEX 8, TI Plus, the Trade360 SaaS model), which lets banks upgrade in place instead of replacing.
Replacement can take years. HSBC took about 3.5 years from selecting CGI to the first two markets going live.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Billing is regulated and revenue-critical, and failed cutovers are publicly costly (LADWP went from $87M to about $181M). SAP's 2027/2030 IS-U deadline forces decade-long replacement contracts, though Kraken's 70M+ cloud accounts show competitive retail energy is migrating faster than municipal water and power.

s1.why: Several primary sources across vendors show the installed cores predate 2005 and run on-prem. The California State Auditor (2014-105) says LADWP's replaced CIS was 40 years old and heavily customised. CPS Energy (San Antonio) has run SAP since 2001 and is retiring it by 2027. Santa Fe, NM ran JD Edwards UCIS on IBM iSeries/AS400 (2016 RFP), and Danbury, CT runs HTE on AS400. SAP IS-U, the dominant large-utility CIS, is an R/3/ECC module from 1998, and SAP's 2027/2030 ECC maintenance end applies to it. Oracle CC&B comes from SPL, which predates its 2006 acquisition. Caveats: no source quantifies installed-base share, the IS-U ship date comes from a consultancy page, and the SE Asian state cores are newer (EVN CMIS 2004, PLN AP2T 2012).

s2.why: Primary sources show multi-year programmes and long contracts. CPS Energy approved a 10-year, $70M Oracle contract to replace its 23-year-old SAP. The total programme is about $304M, with go-lives staged through FY2028 and customer billing in Release 2. LADWP had 3+ years of integration before its 2013 cutover, and costs went from $87M to about $181M (state audit). Santa Fe's 2014 CIS Infinity contract ceased in Oct 2015 with UCIS still live. Danbury's RFP asks for 10-year pricing. Industry commentary puts large IOU CIS programmes at 3-5 years. The evidence is a set of cases, not a survey, but it spans SAP, mainframe and AS/400 bases and is backed by SAP's forced 2027/2030 deadline.

s3.why: The evidence is anecdotal and comes from municipal RFPs and press. Gulfport, MS (Tyler ERP 9, 21 years) cites manual notifications and collections, manual ACH fixes and batch file imports. CPS Energy says its SAP needs 'quite a bit of manual intervention' and many add-on applications. Ogden, UT wants to 'automate many manual processes'. No source names spreadsheets, re-keying at scale or screen-scraping, and nothing quantifies these workarounds across the dominant IS-U or CC&B base. LADWP's post-cutover backlogs describe a failed migration, not a steady-state workaround.

s4.why: Santa Fe had to contract out RPG, CL and DB2/iSeries skills for UCIS, but that is one municipality. GAO-25-107795 on COBOL staff scarcity covers federal systems, not utilities. SAP S/4HANA talent-shortage claims (consulting rates up 30-50%, scarce data-migration and EMIGALL people) come from recruiters and blogs and cover SAP in general, not IS-U. These sources describe a shortage of people who can migrate off the old systems more than a shortage of people who can run them. No primary or quantified source shows that IS-U, CC&B, Banner or Customer/1 skills are scarce.

reasons_to_stay: Billing is regulated and revenue-critical. Failed cutovers cause bill shocks, such as Amarillo's 2026 new system overcharging 55,000+ customers and triggering an $85K audit, and LADWP's post-2013 billing breakdown.
Replacement takes years and gets budgeted as capital: LADWP took 3+ years, Santa Fe's replacement attempt stalled after its 2014 RFP, and Ogden spent a 5-year ERP transition.
Data conversion risk: decades of account history, rate structures and custom code (RPG/CL, COBOL, ABAP) must be migrated.
Deep integration with meter data management, ERP, payments and field service. TNB's CRM, for example, integrates with e-CIBS, ERMS and LGBNet.
Public procurement cycles and multi-year contracts (Danbury asks for 10-year escalation schedules), plus the need to cite peer references converted from the same legacy product.
In Asia, core billing is often built in-house by state utilities (EVN CMIS, PLN AP2T) and is a national standard, so there is no vendor sale to replace.

Manhattan PkMS/WMi is RPG on IBM i from 1990, with 500+ companies on it in 2009. Blue Yonder Dispatcher (mid-1980s) and HighJump (1983) also predate 2005. Caveats: the counts are dated or analyst estimates, and part of the base has already moved to SAP EWM (2006+) and Manhattan Active. The pattern still holds across the dominant vendors, not just one.

s2.why: The multi-year evidence is one government anecdote. DLA's move from the legacy DSS to SAP is running about 2023 to 2026 across 34 sites. Gartner's point that WMS is among the least upgraded applications comes secondhand via SCDigest, and the 15+ year lifespan figure was never verified. The 7+ year contract test fails: Manhattan's 10-K says Active subscriptions typically run 5+ years. No quantified survey of replacement duration across the category was found.

s3.why: Green-screen RF terminal emulation and screen reformatting (Ivanti Velocity, StayLinked) are real and widespread. But Ivanti's 16,000-customer figure is a vendor claim covering all terminal-emulation use, not WMS alone. Spreadsheet figures (for example Kardex's 62% partially integrated, and claims that 40%+ track inventory in spreadsheets) are vendor marketing surveys. They mostly describe warehouses with no WMS, not workarounds around a legacy WMS. No primary source quantifies re-keying around the dominant legacy WMS.

s4.why: Fortra's 2026 IBM i survey (n=315) shows 69% name skills a top concern. That is quantified, but it covers IBM i shops generally, not WMS users, so applying it to WMi or Reflex is an inference. It says nothing about the largest legacy pool, SAP LE-WM, where ABAP and WM consultants remain plentiful. The deadline creates demand for EWM skills; it does not show WM skills are scarce. Dispatcher/MOCA scarcity is anecdotal.

reasons_to_stay: Deep customization. Gartner (via SCDigest) notes that heavy modifications made WMS among the least upgraded applications, with over 50% of post-implementation TCO spent supporting them.
Execution risk. A WMS outage stops shipping. DLA's SAP rollout runs site by site, with brown-outs and go-live windows each spanning months.
Green-screen RF flows are fast and stable, and terminal-emulation modernization (Ivanti Velocity, StayLinked) lets firms reskin them on Android without touching the host WMS.
Vendors keep legacy lines alive. Manhattan still offers SCALE on-prem via perpetual licenses and historically kept RPG staff for WMi.
Tight integration with MHE/automation, ERP and carrier systems built over decades, which must all be re-tested on cutover.
Peak-season constraints limit cutover windows to a few months a year, stretching multi-site programs over years.

name: Wealth and portfolio accounting
systems: SS&C Advent Axys (Windows client-server PMS, REPLANG report language)
SS&C Advent APX and Geneva
FIS Investment Accounting Manager (formerly InvestOne; COBOL, IBM mainframe/CICS origin)
SEI TRUST 3000 (bank trust and investment accounting)
Avaloq Banking Suite / Avaloq Core (private banking and wealth core)
Temenos Triple'A Plus (ex-Odyssey Financial Technologies) and T24 Private Wealth
SimCorp Dimension (front-to-back investment management)
WealthSpectrum by Applied Software (India PMS back office)
Excel/spreadsheet aggregation in family offices
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software at the bank, trust and fund-accounting core: a mainframe COBOL engine (InvestOne) still keeps the books for most mutual funds, and audited performance history is hard to migrate. It is less locked at the RIA and family-office end, where cloud aggregators (Addepar, Orion, Black Diamond) already dominate new installs.

s1.why: Primary, quantified evidence covers the systems that carry most of the book of record. The FIS/Micro Focus case study says InvestOne was built in COBOL on an IBM mainframe in the 1980s and runs over 60% of mutual funds (about $40T). Goldman Sachs' re:Invent 2024 slides (which I extracted and read) confirm InvestOne was licensed in 1991, runs under CICS on the mainframe, and has been GSAM's core for 30 years. SEI's 10-K places TRUST 3000 at 94 US banks. Avaloq (1985) and Advent's 1983 PC/client-server accounting cover private banks and RIAs. One caveat: the US RIA mid-market now runs largely on cloud tools (Orion, Black Diamond, Addepar, Tamarac), so S1 holds for banks, trust departments and fund accounting more than for small advisers.

s2.why: The evidence is a set of single-firm cases plus one vendor's contract terms. Goldman has a ~5-year strategic plan with a 12-month tactical replatform. Julius Baer's Temenos core replacement runs from 2015 to ~2028. SEI's 10-K gives initial terms of 3-7 years for TRUST 3000 and 5-7 years for SEI Wealth Platform, so 7+ is only the upper bound, and the figures date from 2016. The Kitces claim that 60-80% of implementations miss their timeline is secondary and has no method behind it. No category-wide data on replacement duration or contract length was found.

s3.why: The RBC/Campden 2024 report (I extracted and read it) says over-reliance on spreadsheets is the top operational risk for 37% of North American family offices, with manual aggregation close behind. That is a primary source, but it covers the small family-office segment and does not tie the workarounds to Axys, InvestOne, Avaloq or the other dominant systems. The Avaloq survey (45% call their systems outdated) is vendor-sponsored and reported secondhand by finews. Nothing shows re-keying or screen-scraping around the dominant installed systems at scale.

s4.why: The only direct evidence is one firm's slide. Goldman lists 'Difficult finding mainframe skill set' as a challenge for InvestOne, alongside ~$6M a year in mainframe cost and FIS eventually ending mainframe support. That is a generic mainframe-skills point, not specific to this category, and comes from one company. The REPLANG niche and Avaloq certification requirements come from consultant sites and job posts, not from a study of skill shortages.

reasons_to_stay: Book of record and audited performance history live in the old system; conversions risk breaking GIPS-style return series and cost-basis data
60-80% of PMS implementations overrun timelines and costs can revert to list price (Kitces)
Custom reports (REPLANG on Axys/APX) and custom COBOL orchestration layers (Goldman on InvestOne) embed years of firm-specific logic
Vendors offer modernisation without switching: FIS replatformed InvestOne to Linux/containers and 75% of its clients are hosted; SS&C keeps shipping Axys versions
Long 5-7 year contracts and multi-entity core-banking integration (Avaloq, Temenos) tie wealth accounting to the bank core
Regulatory reporting and custodian feeds are already wired and certified
